The work of Henry Cavendish
14
IntroductIon
The British scientist Henry Cavendish devised an ingenious 
method of measuring the gravitational force of attraction 
between two masses in the laboratory. Although he did 
not determine the value of G, the universal gravitational 
constant, his experiments and apparatus enabled others 
to do so. Cavendish was interested in determining the mean 
density of the Earth and he did this using his equipment. 
Aim
To look at some of the experimental work done by 
Cavendish and its use in determining the value of G  
and some related physical values. 
data
Cavendish used a ‘torsion balance’, which consisted of two 
small lead spheres (m = 0.73 kg) on the ends of a rod that 
was suspended from a long wire. As these spheres were 
brought near two large, massive spheres (M = 158.00 kg), 
the attractive gravitational forces caused the rod to rotate 
and so twisted the wire. The extent of the twisting gave a 
measure of the very small attractive force between the 
small and large spheres. The principle of this balance is 
shown in Figure 1. The separation of the centres of the 
spheres (r) was approximately 0.405 m, as shown in 
Figure 2.

The work of James Prescott Joule
16
IntroductIon
Until about 1880 ‘heat’ was considered to be a weightless 
material fluid that flowed from one body to another.  
This fluid was called ‘caloric’. The theory was useful in 
developing ideas about quantities such as heat and 
specific heat capacities. For example, the unit of heat was 
called the ‘calorie’, and was defined as that amount of heat 
that would raise the temperature of 1.0 g of water by 
1.0 Celsius degree. However, evidence from further 
investigations suggested that this theory was not valid 
and that heat, like kinetic and potential energy, was a 
form of energy. James Joule reasoned that if heat was a 
form of energy, then it could be transformed into other 
forms and that there would be a definite ‘conversion 
factor’ according to the Law of Conservation of Energy. 
Joule set out to determine this conversion factor by 
changing mechanical energy into heat energy.
Aim
To collect some data from an experiment similar to Joule’s 
experiment and so calculate the ‘conversion factor’.
data
Joule’s apparatus is shown in Figures 1 and 2. A 
calorimeter was divided into compartments using baffle 
plates, and filled with a known mass of water. The solid 
masses M1 and M2 were wound up to the levels A and C 
respectively and then allowed to drop back through 
height h, to B and D. This caused the paddles in the 
calorimeter to spin and thus transformed the potential 
energy of the masses into heat energy of the water, so 
raising its temperature. This was repeated a number of 
times by winding the masses back up and repeating the 
drop. Any rise in the temperature of the water was 
recorded. Some data derived from such an experiment is 
given below. 
• 
Mass of water in calorimeter = 4.00 kg
• 
Mass of M1 = Mass of M2 = 70.0 kg
• 
Number of times masses were dropped = 20
• 
Distance of drop = 3.0 m
• 
Temperature rise in water = 5.

Torque
13
IntroductIon
The term ‘torque’ is one that is often used in relation to 
forces and their effects. Another term that means the 
same is ‘moment’. The torque or moment of a force is a 
measure of its turning effect about a point. The simple 
actions of turning a key in a lock, opening a door and 
turning a tap on or off all involve torque.
Aim
To understand the meaning of torque and look at some of 
its various applications. 
data: Force at an angle
The torque of a force depends upon (a) the size of the 
force and (b) the perpendicular distance from the line of 
action of the force to its fulcrum or turning point. Hence 
the formula for torque is: 
Torque = Force × Distance (perpendicular)
The symbol for torque is τ, and the SI units are newton 
metres (Nm). Three diagrams are supplied and you are 
asked to determine the torque in each case.

Total internal reflection and optical fibres
25
IntroductIon
Optical fibres are used increasingly in communications 
and medical procedures. 
Aim
To understand some principles used in these fibres which 
enables them to transmit wave motions as they do.
data 
The phenomenon of total internal reflection occurs in 
some situations when light travelling in one medium 
strikes a boundary with a second medium of lower 
refractive index. If the angle of incidence (i) is small, 
refraction occurs as the light pass into the second 
medium (Figure 1). As the angle of incidence is increased, 
a point is reached at which the refracted ray passes along 
the surface of separation of the two media (Figure 2).  
If the angle of incidence is increased beyond this point, 
the light cannot leave the original medium. Instead, it is 
totally reflected within this medium, with the reflection 
obeying the normal laws of reflection (Figure 3). The angle 
of incidence that results in refraction along the surface  
of separation is called the critical angle (θc). It is related  
to the refractive index (RI) of the original medium by 
the relationship:

Wave transmission I
23
IntroductIon
Two basic types of mechanical wave transmission that 
commonly occur are (a) transverse and (b) longitudinal. 
Both types are transmitted in elastic media. The 
longitudinal mechanical waves are transmitted because 
the medium shows some resistance to compression forces 
and so ‘rebounds’ in an elastic manner. The speed of the 
rebound is reflected in the ‘compression modulus’ for the 
medium. The bigger the value of this modulus, the more 
elastic the medium is to compression waves and the 
greater the speed of the waves in it. A similar logic applies 
to mechanical transverse waves in media that are subject 
to shear forces by the waves and so each medium is 
assigned a ‘shear modulus’.
Aim
To investigate aspects of mechanical shear (i.e. transverse) 
waves and their transmission through various media. 
data

determined from the formula

No matter how hard you try, you can only do this one hand at a time.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Place a wooden ruler on top of your two hands so the ends
of the ruler are supported by your two index fingers.
2  Slowly slide your two index fingers towards the centre of
the ruler. (Only one finger at a time will move along the
ruler. The fingers will alternate until they meet at the
balance point of the ruler.)
3  Now try to move both fingers back to their original positions. (Only one finger will move along 
the ruler.)
EXPLANATION
The moving finger is whichever one has the least weight on it and, consequently, the least friction. At any
one time, the amount of weight on each finger will depend on its location relative to the ruler’s centre of
gravity and the turning moments at each finger.
TO INVESTIGATE 
Predict what would happen if you used an irregular object, such as an axe handle or a pool cue, instead 
of a ruler. 
Railway lines are very smooth, but they still do their work by friction. The train engines are so heavy
that there is enough friction between the wheel and the tracks to provide grip.
Friction heat ignites matches.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Feel the force of friction. Take two exercise books and interlock them by alternating at least 20 pages
from each book. Make sure they overlap over at least half their width. Hold the books at the bind and
try to pull them apart. (Friction between the pages will make them very hard to pull apart.)
2  Make a model hovercraft using a balloon, a cotton reel,
some glue and a small sheet of plywood with a hole in the
centre. Blow up the balloon then quickly push the
hovercraft over a smooth surface. (It will seem to glide
because the air from the balloon decreases the friction
between the plywood and the surface below.)

A sound wave can blow out a candle.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Obtain an empty, plastic 2 L milk container and remove 
the lid. 
2  Position the opening of the container about 2cm to one
side of a candle flame.
3  Tap the base of the container with a teaspoon. (The flame
will be extinguished.)
EXPLANATION
The tap on the end of the container produces a compression
wave that travels through the container and is funnelled
through the opening with enough force to blow out the
candle.
TO INVESTIGATE
Cut a hole in the base of a large, plastic garbage bin. Put the
lid on the bin and tap it with your hand. From how far away
can it knock over a polystyrene cup?
Loud sounds can momentarily stun people. This fact is 
used by karate experts, who are trained to shout loudly 
as they fight.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Use a balloon to model thunder. Safety warning: give
others fair warning of the noise and don’t hold it near
anyone’s ear. Blow up a balloon until it is half inflated, then
burst it with a pin.(The air is slightly compressed inside the
balloon, so there will be a bang when it expands rapidly.
This is similar to the way thunder is produced — a bolt of
lightning heats the air around it, which suddenly expands,
and we hear this compression wave as thunder.)
2  Calculate how far away a thunderstorm is. In a thunderstorm, lightning and thunder are produced at
the same time. We see the lightning instantaneously, but it takes time for the sound of thunder to
travel to us. (Sound travels at about 1/3 km/s, so count the number of seconds between seeing the
lightning and hearing the thunder, then divide by 3 to give the distance in kilometres.)

When you have your heels against the wall you cannot touch the floor.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Stand with the backs of your heels firmly against the wall.
2  Try to touch the floor in front of your feet without moving
your feet or bending your knees. (You will not be able to
touch the floor without falling over.)
EXPLANATION
A person’s centre of gravity is usually just above his/her hips.
When you try to touch the floor your centre of gravity moves
in front of both feet and you topple over. 
Tug-of-war teams try to achieve a low centre of gravity. The
five-man tug-of-war was an Olympic event up until 1920.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a tightrope walker. Insert two forks and a match 
into a potato so it balances on a tight string. (Using the
weight of the fork handles, the centre of gravity of the
system will be lowered to just below the string, so the 
potato will not fall off.)
2  Which senses are involved in balance? Close your eyes
then try to balance on one leg. (You will find it extremely
difficult to stay upright. The eyes and the semicircular
canals of the middle ear work together to give you
information about balance.)
Your brain makes you seasick. When your eyes and your middle ear send conflicting messages (as when
you are in a rolling ship), the brain gets confused and floods your body with stress hormones that
make you feel sick. This seems a pointless thing to do and scientists still don’t understand why the
brain does it.

One hand feels warm and the other hand feels cold, but they are both in the same bowl of water.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Set up three empty ice cream containers in a row. Put hot
(but not scalding) water in the first, tepid water in the
second and cold water in the third.
2  Put your left hand in the hot water and your right hand in
the cold water for about 1 minute. Swirl the water a little
with your hands to keep the temperature even.
3  Quickly transfer both hands into the tepid water and
concentrate on what each hand is sensing. (The left hand
will sense cool water, and the right hand will sense warm
water.)
EXPLANATION
Your heat and cold receptors sense changes in temperature rather than absolute temperature. The tepid
water feels cold by comparison with hot water.
Most animals don’t perspire. In fact, humans and horses are among the very few mammals that do use
perspiration to cool themselves. Instead, dogs pant to evaporate water from their tongues (dogs pant
when they are hot rather than ‘puffed’), and kangaroos lick the underside of their wrists where the
blood vessels are near the surface.
Rattlesnakes can locate warm-blooded prey by sensing the heat they give off. Their heat sensors can
detect a temperature increase of 0.002oC.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Use body heat to expand air. Place an empty wine bottle in
the fridge until it is cold. Take it out and place a wet ping-
pong ball in the mouth of the bottle. Wrap both of your
hands  around the bottle. (The air inside the bottle will
expand as it is warmed by your body heat. Some of the air
will leave the bottle, causing the ball to plop up and down
in the opening.)
2  Feel heat conduction. Use your hand to compare the
temperature of a metal chair leg and a wooden table top.
(The metal will feel colder because the heat from your hand
is rapidly conducted away. The wood will feel warmer
because it is a poor conductor, so the heat from your hand is
not dissipated.)

One student can exert more force than two students.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Get two people to each hold a broomstick, about 1m apart.
2  Tie the end of a rope to one of the sticks, then wind the rope
three times around both sticks, as shown in the diagram. 
3  Ask a third person to pull the rope while the other two try to stay
where they are. Safety warning: fingers should be kept clear of the

The sticks and rope are like a simple block and tackle. A block and tackle with four pulleys uses one
quarter of the force normally needed to lift the object. However, in the activity above, friction will

A floating pen top can be made to sink and then rise without being touched.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Attach some plasticine to a plastic pen top, so that it only
just floats in water. Be careful not to block the opening of
the pen top.
2  Lower the pen top into a plastic bottle filled with water.
3  Screw the lid on tightly, then squeeze the sides of the
bottle. (The pen top will sink when you squeeze the bottle
and rise again when you stop squeezing.)
EXPLANATION
When you squeeze the bottle the water transfers the pressure
to the air inside the pen top. The air inside the pen top
becomes compressed, so the unit (air pocket + pen top)
becomes more dense than the water, and it sinks.
TO INVESTIGATE
Can you find any evidence that the air inside the pen top
becomes compressed when you squeeze the bottle? (You can
observe it if you look into the pen top from below.)

Water travels surprisingly quickly up a celery stalk.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Take a gas jar and pour some red food colouring into it 
(a depth of 0.5cm is enough). Do not dilute the food
colouring.
2  Cut a fresh celery stalk with its leaves still attached and put
the lower end of the stalk into the dye. Place it in a warm
sunny position. Record the time. 
3 Remove the stalk after 3 minutes and progressively cut up
the stalk to see how far the dye has gone. (The dye should
have travelled right up the stem.)
EXPLANATION
The coloured water travels up the xylem vessels in the stalk by adhesive forces (between the water and the
walls of the vessels) and cohesive forces (between the water molecules). Evaporation from the leaves
maintains the flow.
The Australian mountain ash (Eucalyptus regnans) is the
tallest flowering plant in the world. Water travels upwards
over 90 m in some of these trees.

firewood log in which the growth rings are clearly visible.
Count the rings and compare their widths. (Many trees
produce one growth ring each year. Wide rings indicate
years of high rainfall or warm temperatures, with
consequent greater growth.)

When corn kernels are put in fizzy water they go up and down.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Put about a dozen kernels of popping corn in a 200mL
beaker of water. (They will sink.)
2  Put an antacid tablet in the water, wait for it to finish
fizzing and then observe the corn. (The corn kernels will
rise to the surface and then sink many times over the next
few minutes.)
EXPLANATION
The corn kernel by itself is more dense than water, so it sinks.
However, the surface of the kernel provides sites for bubbles
of carbon dioxide to form. The average density of the
corn–bubble unit is lower than that of water, so it rises to the
surface. The bubbles burst, and the process is repeated.
TO INVESTIGATE
Does this phenomenon apply only to corn and antacid? Try
‘hundreds and thousands’ and currants; and try other types of
carbonated drinks.
Pumice is a rock that floats, and ebony is a wood 
that sinks.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Do the rotten egg test. Let an egg go rotten, then place it in
a beaker of water with a fresh egg. (The fresh egg will sink,
but the rotten egg will float because gases are produced by
bacteria as they decompose the contents of the egg.)
2  Make an egg float in acid. Safety glasses and laboratory
coats should be worn. Place a fresh egg in a beaker and add
dilute hydrochloric acid until the beaker is almost full. (The
egg will initially sink, but will then rise to the surface as the
acid reacts with the calcium carbonate in the shell of the egg
to produce bubbles of carbon dioxide.)

You can squash a surprising amount of cotton wool into a beaker of water. 
HOW TO DO IT
1  Tightly pack cotton wool into a small beaker until it
reaches the 100mL mark. 
2  Remove the cotton wool from the beaker and replace it
with exactly 100mL of water. 
3  Slowly add all the cotton wool to the beaker, pushing it
down firmly with a pencil to remove all the air. Make sure
that none of the cotton wool is above the surface. (The
water level will only rise 3–4mL.)
EXPLANATION
Materials that contain a lot of air are usually good insulators.
Cotton wool consists mainly of air, and the amount of cotton
is relatively small. When cotton wool is submerged, the water
replaces the air, and the slight rise in the water level
represents the solid portion.
Emperor penguins have to stand on the bare ice throughout
the long Antarctic winter, yet they have absolutely no
insulation on their feet. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Insulate an ice block. Wrap an ice block in a large sheet of newspaper and secure it with a rubber
band. Place another ice block on a dish, uninsulated. Compare the rates of melting. (Air trapped in the
newspaper will insulate the first piece of ice from the heat in the room.)
2  Investigate insulation in cups. Obtain a polystyrene cup
and a tin cup of about the same size. Fill both with water
and put two ice cubes in each. Compare the rates of
melting of the ice. (The polystyrene contains air, which
insulates the contents, so the ice will melt more slowly.)

You can make fog come out of a beaker of water.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY
1  Half fill a very large beaker with water.
2  Add about a dessertspoonful of dry ice. Safety warning: do
not touch the dry ice with your bare hands. (A dense white
fog will emerge from the beaker and spread across the floor.)
EXPLANATION
This activity involves three states of water and two states of carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide changes
from a solid to a gas and bubbles out of the water. As it is denser than air it accumulates near the floor of
the room. The carbon dioxide gas is very cold, so it cools the air around it, causing water vapour to
condense into droplets. Meanwhile, some of the liquid water in the beaker will have turned into ice as it
was frozen by the dry ice.
A whale’s spout is not a stream of water — it is just air
that has been blown out of its lungs. The air is warm and
moist from the lungs and when it hits the cooler, outer air
the water vapour in it condenses into fog.
Any known substance that can be heated to its boiling
point will evaporate. Iron evaporates at about 2900oC.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Does this can leak? Fill a tin can with icewater. Observe the
outside of the can. (The cold metal cools the air in contact
with it. As the air cools, the water vapour in it condenses
and will appear as drops on the outside of the can.)
2  Change the state of cola. TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY — Safety glasses and laboratory coats
should be worn. Pour half a can of cola into a flask and attach it to a condenser. Predict what sort of
liquid will be collected from the condenser when the cola is boiled. (Cola is about 90% water by
volume, which will be collected by evaporation and condensation. A can of cola also contains, among
other things, about 6 teaspoons of sugar, kola nut extracts for flavour and carbon dioxide for
effervescence.)

You can make a daisy turn green.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Obtain a yellow daisy and cut the stem so it is only 5–6cm
long.
2  Place the cut end of the stem in a small beaker containing
some undiluted blue food colouring.
3  Put the beaker and flower in a warm sunny part of the room. (After a few minutes the blue colour will
begin to appear in the petals. As more dye enters the petals they will eventually turn green.)
EXPLANATION
The food colouring travels up the xylem vessels in the stem of the plant and enters the petals. The green
colour results from the combination of the yellow petals and the blue dye.
TO INVESTIGATE
Does this phenomenon apply only to daisies? Also, is it possible to colour a flower with two different
colours?
Not all flowers are sweet smelling. The stinking corpse lily
(Rafflesia), of Malaysian jungles, is the world’s largest
flower, growing up to 1 m in diameter. It makes a smell like
rotting meat to attract flies to pollinate it.
Not all insect visitors at flowers are collecting nectar. 
Some orchids have their petals arranged in such a way as 
to resemble a female wasp. Male wasps are attracted to the
flowers and try to mate with them, but they only succeed 
in pollinating the flowers.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Dissect an orchid. Obtain a large orchid and identify the
features which make it different to other flowers. (Orchid
flowers are vertically symmetrical. The sepals are coloured,
the lower petal forms a lip that is a landing platform for
insects, and the male and female parts are combined into a
column inside the flower. Any insect that lands on the lip
and falls into the centre of the flower will brush against the
column, resulting in pollination.)
2  Have a scavenger hunt for plant reproductive structures
that don’t have petals. During spring, find the flowers of
grasses, eucalypts and bottle brushes plus the reproductive
structures of conifers, ferns and mosses.

A cup with a hole in it will lose water, but not if it is in free fall.
HOW TO DO IT
This activity should be done outside.
1  Fill a polystyrene cup with water. Use a pen to put a hole
near the bottom of the cup. (The water will drain out.)
2  Place your finger over the hole and fill the cup again.
3  Hold the cup up high and let it drop to the ground. (The
water will not come out of the hole while the cup is falling.)
EXPLANATION
The force of gravity makes the water drain from the cup when it is held in the air. When the cup is falling,
both the water and the cup are accelerating at the same rate so the water is apparently weightless in
comparison to the cup.
Astronauts train for weightlessness in space by moving
around and ‘floating’ inside a diving aeroplane
(affectionately referred to as the ‘vomit comet’). The
apparent weightlessness that space shuttle astronauts
experience in space is actually caused by the same
phenomenon — the craft is continuously falling in a curved
path around the earth.
In 1944, an airman fell out of a Lancaster bomber at an
altitude of 5 km and lived.
If a bullet is fired from a gun that is horizontal, it will hit
the ground at the same time as another bullet which is
simply dropped from that height.

You can make a metal pin stay on top of the water.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Fill a beaker with water up to its pouring spout.
2  At the pouring spout, gently place the head of a dry, clean
pin onto the surface of the water.
3  Give the sharp end a gentle tap with your fingernail so the
pin slides out onto the surface of the water. (The pin will
remain on top of the water.) 
EXPLANATION
The force of attraction (cohesive force) between the molecules at the surface of the water is strong enough
to support a pin. 
TO INVESTIGATE
Do other liquids have surface tension? Try salt water, warm water, cooking oil and methylated spirits.
Safety warning: be careful of methylated spirits’ fumes. (Surface tension is usually lower in warm water and
organic liquids.) 
The pin in the activity above was not wet. It was not actually in the water. It was on top of the water
and was therefore still dry.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Confuse a matchstick. Half fill a small (100mL) beaker
with water. Drop a small piece of match stick (5mm long)
into the middle of the water. (It will move towards the glass
because the meniscus curves upwards there, and the stick
floats to the highest point of the water.) Now fill the beaker
above its rim and float the stick next to the glass. (It will
move away from the glass because surface tension holds the
water in, and the highest point of the water is now in the
middle.)
2  Water a coin. Put a single drop of water on a 5c coin and
use it to predict how many drops of water you could fit on
the coin. Use a pipette to administer 1 drop at a time until
the water overflows. (Surface tension will hold more water
on the coin than most people predict.)

This apple will sink in hot water but float in cold water.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Obtain a fresh apple and some large nails. Embed enough
nails in the underside of the apple so that it will only just
float in cold water. 
2  Place the apple in a large beaker of cold water. (The apple
will float.)
3  Place the apple in a large beaker of hot water. (The apple will sink.)
4  Add cold water to the beaker with the sunken apple. (The apple will rise to the surface.)
EXPLANATION
The hot water is less dense than the cold water (because water expands when it is heated), so the hot
water has less upthrust. (Upthrust is reduced in fluids of lower density.)
Heat causes the sea to expand. The El Niño effect is caused
by a large pool of relatively warm water (5–10oC higher
than normal) located in the eastern Pacific. Because this
water is warm, it has expanded, so sea levels along the
coast of South America can be up to 25 cm higher than
usual.
Some types of bacteria live in boiling water in hot springs. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make an underwater convection current. Take a small vial,
add a few drops of food colouring and fill it to the brim
with hot water. Place it in a large beaker of cold water. (The
coloured water is warmer and less dense, so it will move to
the top of the beaker.)
Underwater volcanoes make the continents move. Australia will have moved over 4 m northwards during
your lifetime.
2  Expand a bottle. Fill a plastic bottle with water and screw the lid on tightly. Place it in the freezer
overnight. (Water expands as it freezes, so the bottle will be swollen or cracked in the morning.)

An egg will sink in one beaker of water but float in another.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Gently place a fresh egg in a beaker
of tap water. (The egg will sink.)
2  Transfer the egg to a beaker of very
salty water. (The egg will float.)
EXPLANATION
Salt water is more dense than fresh water. The buoyancy force (or upthrust) is greater in fluids of higher
density. In salt water there is enough upthrust for the egg to float.
TO INVESTIGATE
Predict how the weights of equal volumes of the salt water and tap water used in this activity would
compare. Use a volumetric pipette to measure volumes and a digital balance to compare weights;
calculate their densities.
The oceans came from rocks. The space rocks that originally formed the earth contained small amounts of
water chemically combined with minerals in the rocks. When the rocks melted in the interior of the
earth, the water was released as steam, which emerged from volcanoes and eventually formed the oceans. 
When salt water freezes, the salt is forced out, so the ice is fresh water.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make an ice block sink. TEACHER
DEMONSTRATION ONLY — Put one
ice block in water and another one in
methylated spirits. Safety warning: be
careful of fumes. (Water is more dense
than methylated spirits, so the ice will
float in the former and sink in the
latter.)
2  Separate salt water from fresh water. Half fill a beaker
with very salty water then float an egg in it. Slowly and
gently add fresh water to the side of the beaker until it is
full. (The two liquids do not fully mix, so the egg will remain
halfway up the beaker at their interface.)
Some parts of the sea are fresh water. Fresh water and salt water don’t automatically mix, so when the
water from the Amazon River enters the Atlantic Ocean it continues as a body of fresh water for
100 km out to sea.

It’s easy to tell the difference between gold and fool’s gold.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Rub a piece of white paper on a gold ring. (The gold will
not leave a mark on the paper.)
2  Rub a piece of white paper on some fool’s gold  (iron
pyrites). (A black mark will appear on the  paper.)
EXPLANATION
Iron pyrites (FeS2) is a compound containing iron and sulfur,
so its properties are quite different to those of gold. This
activity is an example of a streak test, in which the colour of a
streak of the mineral can be used to help identify it.
There is no gold in our Australian ‘gold’ coins. One dollar and two dollar coins are 92% copper, 6%
aluminium and 2% nickel. 
There are hundreds of kilograms of gold in each cubic kilometre of seawater, but we have not yet
found a profitable way to extract it.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Model gold panning. Place a mixture of sand and lead shot
in a bowl. Run some tapwater into the bowl. Tip the bowl
slightly to one side and swirl it so that some of the water
and sand leaves the bowl. Repeat this a few times until
there is only lead shot in the bowl. (Lead shot, like gold, is
more dense than sand, so it sinks more rapidly in the
moving water and will thus remain in the bowl.)
2  Model the carat in gold rings. (Twenty-four carat gold is
pure. Other carat numbers indicate the proportion of gold
out of a total of 24. Eighteen carat gold is 18 parts gold and
6 parts copper; 12 carat gold is half gold and half copper.
The copper is added to make the gold harder.) Use lemon
jelly mixture to represent gold and gelatine to represent
copper. For example, a 12 carat mixture would be half jelly
mixture and half gelatine; pure gold would be jelly mixture
only. (The more gelatine in the mixture the harder the jelly
will become.)

There are sounds you cannot hear.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Use a sound frequency generator to find a sound all the
students in the class can hear comfortably. 
2  Tell all the students to put their hands in the air and only
lower them when they cannot hear the sound any more.
Increase the frequency until most, but not all, of the
students cannot hear it. 
3  Demonstrate that it is possible to increase the frequency to
much higher levels that no-one can hear.
EXPLANATION
Humans can only hear sounds up to about 20,000 Hz. Most of
the sounds grasshoppers, dolphins and bats make are well
above 20,000 Hz. As you get older, the range of sounds you
can hear decreases.
Dogs and cats can hear many sounds we cannot. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Enhance your hearing. Stand 2–3m away from a ticking clock. Face the clock and cup your hands
behind your ears. (The ticking will appear to be slightly louder. The outer ear of humans plays little or
no role in helping us hear, but ear trumpets and other sound collection devices can effectively increase
audibility.)
2  Dramatise echolocation by bats. This activity should be
done  outside in a flat open area free of obstacles. Mark out
an open space about 3m square. Nominate one student to
be the bat and another to be the moth, which tries to
escape. The bat is blindfolded. Every time the bat says
“bat” the moth must say “moth” (so if the bat says ‘Bat-
bat-bat-bat . . .’ in rapid succession the moth must reply
every time). (Even though he/she cannot see, the bat will
find it surprisingly easy to catch the moth, and thereby
demonstrate  the effectiveness of this hunting technique.)

You can use a magnifying lens to burn wood.
HOW TO DO IT
Safety warning: never look directly at the sun, as this may cause
permanent eye damage.
1  Hold a convex lens in direct sunlight, so the rays are
focused onto a dark piece of wood. 
2  Move the lens up and down until the spot of light is as
small as possible, then move the lens a few millimetres
further away from the wood. (The wood will turn black and
begin to smoke.)
EXPLANATION
Light rays and infra-red heat rays travel from the sun. As they enter the convex lens they become refracted
so they begin to converge. The focal point is where the rays meet. The focal point for heat is slightly
further from the lens than the focal point for light.
The heat and light in this activity were produced in the centre of the sun and took over 100,000 years
to travel to its surface, then about 8 minutes to travel the 150 million kilometres to earth.
The centre of the earth is hotter than the surface of the sun.
Just before the sun dies it will expand until its surface almost reaches the earth. This will destroy all
life on our planet. Don’t worry though, because it won’t happen for another 5 billion years.
LINKED ACTIVITIES

put four match heads next to the wick. Cover the candle with a large beaker. Use a convex lens to focus
direct sunlight onto the match heads. (The match heads will ignite, and so will the candle.)
2  Use water to burn wood. TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY
Fill a round-bottomed flask with water and seal it. Use it to
focus direct sunlight onto a dark piece of wood. (The heat will
be focussed onto the wood by the water in the flask.)

A burning teabag will float into the air.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY Safety glasses and
laboratory coats should be worn.
1 Remove the string and the staple from a teabag, empty the 
tea from it and unfold it to form a cylinder about 10cm long. 
2 Stand the cylinder upright on a dish and use a match to light it all the way around the top rim, so it
burns evenly all the way down. If the teabag starts to topple over then use the spent match to lightly
support it at the side. (As the burning proceeds down towards the dish the teabag will suddenly lift 
1–2m into the air.)
EXPLANATION
The heat from the burning teabag causes the air above it to
rise. When most of the material of the teabag has burned away
it becomes light enough to be lifted into this convection
current that has formed above it.
It is difficult for aeroplanes to take off from high altitude airports on hot days. The reduction in air
pressure, caused by both the high altitude and the expansion of air due to heat from the runway,
means that some aeroplanes can only take off if they are half empty.
Dick Smith crossed Australia in a hot air balloon. He has been referred to as ‘Australia’s answer to
Leonardo da Vinci’ because he was also the first person to circumnavigate the world in a helicopter,
and to reach the North Pole by helicopter. He hasn’t owned Dick Smith Electronics since 1982.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Model a hot air balloon. Obtain a kitchen freezer bag and use a hairdryer to fill it with hot air. Turn the
hairdryer off then release the bag. (The bag will rise above your head because the  warm air inside is less
dense than the surrounding air.)
2  Make a twister. Cut a circle of paper about 15cm in
diameter, then cut into it turning it into a spiral. Tie a
length of cotton to the centre and let it hang a few
centimetres above a hot plate. (The convection currents will
start it spinning.)

You can make other colours come out of a spot of black ink.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Cut a thin strip of filter paper about 15cm long.
2  Use a water soluble felt pen to put a spot of black ink about
2cm from one end. Dab the pen several times on the spot
so there is plenty of ink on it. 
3  Position the end of the filter paper in some water in a beaker but make sure the ink spot is not in the
water. (The ink will move upwards and various colours will appear.)
EXPLANATION
Black ink consists of a mixture of several different-coloured pigments. These pigments have differing
solubilities, and the more soluble ones are carried further up the filter paper by the water.
TO INVESTIGATE
What colours would you find in green, pink, orange and brown water-soluble felt pens? Do all black inks
contain the same pigments?
Some pigments can take on more than one colour. Hydrangeas can be pink or blue, depending on the
acidity of the soil. It is the pigment that changes colour in response to pH.
The primary colours of inks and paints are red, blue and yellow, but the primary colours of light are
red, blue and green.

a brown Smartie to a strip of filter paper, close to one end.

dissolve in the water and the pigments will separate.)

This ink will only appear when it is heated.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY 
Safety warning: this activity requires a safe method of disposing
of sheets of paper that have accidentally ignited.
1  Dip the wooden end of a match stick into some lemon
juice then write with it onto a sheet of paper.
2  Let the lemon juice dry on the paper. (The writing will be
almost invisible.)
3  Hold the sheet of paper very close to an electric radiator,
but not so close that the paper burns. (The lemon juice will
darken and become visible.)
EXPLANATION
The lemon juice contains sugar and other carbon compounds. Upon heating, these begin to break down
and some of the carbon appears by itself. Pure carbon is black, so the colour of the lemon juice slowly gets
darker as more and more carbon appears.
The charcoal on barbecued meat contains a substance 
that causes cancer.
LINKED ACTIVITIES 
1  Make carbon from sugar. TEACHER DEMONSTRATION
ONLY This activity must be carried out in a fume cupboard.
Safety glasses, laboratory coat and acid-proof gloves should be
worn. Add powdered sugar to a 200mL beaker until it is
about half full. Pour in about 10mL of concentrated sulfuric
acid. (The carbon will become separated from the hydrogen
and oxygen in the sugar and, within a few minutes a block of
carbon will rise up from the beaker. Sulfur dioxide fumes will
also be produced.)
2  Make carbon disappear. Safety glasses and
laboratory coats should be worn. Use tongs to
hold a white crucible in a candle flame for a
moment, so that a light streak of soot is
deposited on its outer surface. Then position it
above a blue Bunsen flame. (The soot will
slowly disappear as the hotter flame causes the
complete combustion of the carbon.)

You can make a soup ladle sound like a gong.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Tie the handle of a metal soup ladle to the middle of a 1m
length of string.
2  Hold the two free ends of the string firmly to the openings
of your ears, letting the ladle hang between them.
3  Ask your partner to tap the cup of the ladle with a pencil.
(You will hear a deep ringing sound like a gong, but your
partner will not.)
EXPLANATION
The ladle has a rounded metallic shape like a gong or a bell. You hear the sound loudly because the sound
travels more quickly through the solid string than through the air.
TO INVESTIGATE
Would the sound be different if you used a teaspoon or a tablespoon instead of the ladle? What would two
spoons together sound like?
Sound travels 15 times faster through solid steel than through the air. This is why noises in the school
central heating pipes are often clearly heard in other parts of the school.
Some low-pitched sounds made by whales and dolphins can
travel over 100 km under the water. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a string telephone by connecting two polystyrene
cups with a length of string. Compare the sound
transmission over 10m of string with that over 2m.
Compare the sound transmission in a multi-channel link-
up with four cups connected together. What happens if the
string goes around a corner? 
2  Set up a domino model of sound travel. Make two lines of
dominoes standing on edge. In one line, the dominoes
should be packed together so they are touching each other
(to represent a solid) but in the other line they should be
spaced apart (to represent a gas). The lines should be
exactly the same length. Tip the first domino in each line.
(The ‘chain reaction’ will be faster where the dominoes are
packed together.)

A floating match will suddenly spring away from your finger.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Fill a beaker with water and gently place half a
matchstick onto the surface of the water. (You will be
able to see water adhering to the matchstick.)
2  Put a small drop of liquid soap on the tip of your
finger and touch this ‘magic finger’ to the surface of
the water to one side of the match. (The matchstick
will suddenly spring away from your finger.) 
EXPLANATION
This activity demonstrates the tension in surface tension. The soap weakened the surface tension on one
side of the match. The match sprang away because the surface tension on the other side was stronger (like
a wire under tension will spring away from the point where you cut it).
TO INVESTIGATE
Is it possible to repeat this activity using the same water? (No, you will need to use fresh water and a new
match and remove all the soap in the beaker before you can repeat the activity.)
Some beetles (Stenus) walk slowly on the surface of
mountain streams. But when threatened, they dab the
end of their abdomen on the water and release a
chemical that lowers the surface tension so
dramatically they are whisked away almost faster
than the eye can see.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a soap-powered boat. Cut out a small boat shape
from light cardboard. Cut a notch in the back and fit a
small flake of soap into it, then put the boat in fresh tap
water. (The boat will move forward because the surface
tension is lowered at the back.) 
2  Design a big-bubble recipe. Try mixing different ratios of dishwashing liquid, water and either sugar or
glycerine or gelatine. (When surface tension is weakened, the distance between the water molecules can
be increased to form bubbles. Substances such as sugar, glycerine and gelatine help to make the bubbles
last longer because they form weak adhesive bonds with water. This helps to slow down the rate of
evaporation of the water from the large surface area of the bubbles. A good bubble mixture is one part
dish

You can create an image in mid-air.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Insert a slide into a projector and adjust the lens so that the picture is focused at about 1m in front of
the projector. Take the screen away.
2  Hold a ruler 1m in front of the projector and move it quickly from side to side. (You will see the full
picture where you are waving the ruler.)
EXPLANATION
At each position of the ruler, a part of the picture can be seen
on it. When you wave the ruler these images succeed each
other rapidly and your brain ‘sees’ the current image as well
as the one it already held from a fraction of a second before. It
puts them together to create the illusion of seeing the whole
picture.
A high speed camera can photograph a bullet in flight.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a cartoon by drawing a sequence of pictures, each
one slightly different to the last, on the pages of an exercise
book. Then flip the pages. (When the pictures are presented
in rapid succession it will create the illusion of smooth
motion.) 
2  Put the bird in the cage. Cut out a piece of plain cardboard
about the size of a playing card. Draw the bird on one side
and the cage on the other. Tie a rubber band to each end of
the card, wind it up tightly, then let it unwind. (As the card
rapidly unwinds, the bird will appear to be in the cage.)

You can make mosquito wrigglers dive on command.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Collect some mosquito wrigglers from some stagnant
water (look in ponds, drains, puddles, old buckets, old 44
gallon drums etc.) and put about six in a beaker of fairly
clear water. 
2  Leave the wrigglers undisturbed until they come to the
surface and hang by their breathing tubes. 
3 Tap the beaker with a pencil. (The wrigglers will dive.)
EXPLANATION
Mosquito wrigglers respond to vibrations by diving, probably to avoid predators. However, after
continued stimulation, they do not respond as readily.
TO INVESTIGATE
What other stimuli will make wrigglers dive? (Try dipping a pencil into the water, a sharp clap, blowing on
the water or passing a shadow over the beaker.) Also, how deep can wrigglers dive?
If you get bitten by a mosquito, then you know it was a
female. Male mosquitoes feed only on flower nectar.
Butterflies look fragile, but they have existed in their
present form for millions of years longer than humans.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Resuscitate some ants. Put some large ants in a jar, cool
the jar until the ants are motionless, then place it on an
overhead projector. (All the chemical reactions in living
things are controlled by enzymes, which decrease in activity
as the temperature drops below their optimal level. As the
ants are warmed by the projector they will become active
again and can be observed on the screen.)
2  Observe predation. Place a praying mantis in a jar with
some small branches to climb on. Add a few small living
insects. (The mantis will readily strike at them.)
During mating, the female praying mantis usually kills and eats the male.

uploads/science/Demonstration Guides/Gen.searchText:
Some patterns of lines can fool your brain.
HOW TO DO IT
Answer the questions below, first by using a sight estimation and then by measuring with a ruler.
Are these lines parallel? 
Is one person taller? 
Is this vase taller than it is wide?
EXPLANATION
The brain automatically makes corrections to the images it
receives from the eye and this helps us to interpret our
surroundings. (For example, as objects get further away they
look smaller, but we understand that they are still the same
size.) But when unusual images are presented to the brain, it
can give us the wrong information. 
A young baby’s head makes up about one-quarter of the
length of its body. In some parts of Africa, a child is
deemed to be old enough to begin school when he/she 
can put one arm over his/her head and touch the other
shoulder. Younger children’s heads are too big to allow
them to do this.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Use only one eye to estimate distance. Close your right eye
and hold up a finger from your right hand, about half a
metre in front of your body. Position your left hand about
the same distance away, but much further to the left.
Slowly move a finger from your left hand towards your
right hand finger  and try to touch it. (At the first attempt
you will probably miss because we normally use both eyes to
estimate distance.)
2  Measure your body. Use a length of cotton to measure the circumference of your wrist. Compare this
with the circumference of your neck. (The length will be roughly twice as long.) Is there another body
part that is twice as long again?
Astronauts get taller when they are in space. This is because there is no effect of gravity, so the discs
between their vertebrae are not compressed as much.

You can heat water in a paper container.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY Safety glasses and laboratory coat should be worn. 
1  Use photocopier paper to make a paper tray with a base of about 10cm square and sides about 3–4cm
high. Try to avoid puncturing the paper. 
2  Half fill it with water, then place it on a gauze mat and tripod. 
3  Heat it with a Bunsen. (The paper will not burn.) Safety warning: the paper may disintegrate as 
the water approaches boiling, so it is important to turn the Bunsen off well before this point.)
EXPLANATION
Most of the heat is conducted to the water, so the paper does not reach its ignition temperature.
Diamond is the best thermal conductor. Silver is a better thermal conductor than copper. 
The heat in the interior of the earth is mainly produced by
radioactivity.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Heat water in a balloon. Pour some water into an empty
balloon, then blow it up with the water inside and tie the
opening. Lower the base of the balloon onto a candle
flame. (The heat is conducted to the water, so the balloon
will not burst.)
2  Feel heat conduction. Hold a sewing needle at the blunt
end, and position its point in a candle flame. (After a few
moments you will feel the heat which has been conducted
through the needle.) Safety warning: the needle will quickly
become too hot to hold, so be ready to place it on a heat mat
before it burns you.

You can light a candle without touching the wick.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Secure a candle in a stable position and light it.
2  Strike another match and have it ready.
3  Blow the candle out and immediately hold the burning
match 1–2cm directly above the top of the wick. (The wick
will relight.)
EXPLANATION
Candle wax exists as solid, liquid and gas. Immediately after you have blown out the candle there is still
some paraffin gas near the wick. This gas ignites when a flame is brought near it. 
TO INVESTIGATE
How does the appearance of paraffin change as it turns from a liquid to a solid? (It changes from clear to
white.)
Liquid petrol doesn’t burn — the vapour does. But don’t try to test this because the vapour will always
be there. Safety warning: petrol is extremely dangerous and should never be near a naked flame.
Liquid water is common on earth but is one of the rarest substances in the universe.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Keep tissues dry under water. Crumple a tissue and place
it inside a beaker. Invert the beaker and place it in water.
(The tissue will remain dry because air prevents water from
entering the beaker.)
2  Pour a beaker of air. Add water to a very large beaker until
it is almost full. Hold two small beakers inverted under the
water — the first containing air and the second containing
water. Hold the first beaker directly below the second and
slowly tilt it. (The gas will be transferred to the second
beaker.)

You can make corn seeds explode.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY 
Safety glasses and laboratory coat should be worn.
1  Obtain a large beaker and clean it thoroughly.
2  Cover the bottom of the beaker with about 4 tablespoons
of cooking oil.
3  Place the beaker on a hotplate.
4  Add about 1/2 a cup of popping corn and 1/2 a teaspoon of salt, then cover the beaker.
5  Mix the contents regularly as it heats. (After a few minutes the corn will pop.)
EXPLANATION
Corn seeds contain a small amount of water that is mixed with the starch. When this water is heated it
eventually turns into steam, but the steam is trapped inside the seed by the hard outer coat. The steam
pressure builds up until the kernel explodes, exposing the starch in a frothy state.
TO INVESTIGATE
Do popping corn kernels germinate as readily as corn from seed packets? 
The kangaroo rat and the flour beetle obtain ALL their water from food such as seeds. They never drink.
Some seeds can remain alive for many hundreds of years. Even wheat seeds found inside the Egyptian
pyramids have sprouted when watered.
Peach pits contain cyanide.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Simulate a bushfire. TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY
Safety glasses and laboratory coat should be worn. Hold a
mature banksia cone in a Bunsen flame for a few minutes.
(The seed pods will slowly open and the winged seeds can be
removed. The seeds have a better chance of growing after a
bushfire because competing plants have been destroyed.)
2  Compare the energy in two nuts. Safety glasses and
laboratory coats should be worn. Weigh a pecan nut, then
hold it in position with a pin and light it with a match. Use
the burning nut to heat a small amount of water in a test
tube. Measure the change in temperature of the water.
Repeat the above, using a peanut. (Nuts are seeds that are
extremely rich in proteins, minerals and vitamins; their oil
content burns readily.)

If you roll this can away, it will come back to you.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Obtain a can with a lid. Put two nail holes about 1cm apart
on the base of the can, close to the centre. Also do this with
the lid. 
2  Connect the holes with string as shown in the diagram. 
3  Attach a heavy fishing sinker to the centre of the string.
4  Gently roll the can on a hard, level surface. (The can will
roll to a stop about 1m away and then roll back to you.)
EXPLANATION
As the can rolls away from you, the lead weight does not roll,
so the string winds up. In this way, kinetic energy is changed
to potential energy, which is stored as tension in the string
and a slightly higher position of the weight. When the can rolls
back, the potential energy is converted to kinetic energy.
Window glass is highly elastic over short distances because
it always springs back to exactly where it was.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a mouse trap car. Attach one end of a length of
string to the spring lever of the mouse trap, and wind the
other end around the front axle of the car. (As the trap
closes, the potential energy in the spring is converted to
kinetic energy. This movement pulls the string, which is
wound around the axle, so the car will move forward.)
2  Solve the following problem. Use elastic potential energy
to make a milk carton boat move across a tub of water.
(One possible solution is shown.)

You can make a musical note by rubbing a wineglass.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Put a crystal wineglass on the table and hold it by the neck
rather than the base.
2  Wet a finger and rub it smoothly in one direction around
the rim of the wineglass. (With a bit of practice a musical
note will be heard.)
EXPLANATION
The rubbing causes vibrations in the glass. When these
vibrations match the natural frequency of vibration of the
wineglass, the glass will vibrate at that frequency (that is,
resonate).
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum, so outer space is
always silent.
Some people believe that plants respond to music and there
have even been PhD theses written about it. The results of
one study showed that many flowers prefer classical music
and jazz, definitely do not like loud rock music and are
unaffected by country and western.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Rattle a needle. Obtain two wineglasses that both make exactly the same note. (You may need to add
water to one to change its note.) Stand a sewing needle in one of the glasses. Wet your finger and rub
the rim of the other glass, which should be very close to but not touching the first glass. (The first glass
will resonate and its vibrations will make the needle rattle against the glass.)
2  Use resonance to amplify sounds. Tie a length of string to
the base of a polystyrene cup. Pull the string taut to the
cup and stroke it with the skin of your fingertip. Then let
the string go slack and stroke it. (The sound will only be
audible when the vibrations are transferred to the cup by
taut string. The sound waves reflect and rejoin inside the
cup to become amplified.)

Your eyes can double your money.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Hold two $2 coins about the length of this page from your
eyes, one coin in each hand. 
2  Look past them to the wall of the room. (You will see four
coins.)
EXPLANATION
When we look at an object, each eye sees it from a slightly
different angle and this gives us stereoscopic vision. Our brain
interprets the information the eyes send to it but can
sometimes make mistakes, especially when depth perception
is involved (as in the activity above).
Many spiders have eight eyes.
The closest star to earth cannot be seen with the naked eye. Proxima Centauri is a relatively dim star
that is only slightly bigger than the planet Jupiter. 
The furthest a person can see is about 2 million light years. This is the distance to Andromeda, a
neighbouring galaxy, which is visible on a clear night.
Blindness or partial blindness affects 28 million people worldwide.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  See through a matchbox. Collect a cardboard tube from a toilet roll, put it to one eye and read this
sentence through it with both eyes open. Now hold a matchbox in front of your other eye. (You will
seem to be reading through a hole in the matchbox.)
2  Spot a spook. Stare intently at this picture for about
1 minute without moving your eyes. Then look up at the
bare ceiling and stare fixedly at one part of it. (You will see
an ‘after-image’ of the  ghost. Overstimulation by staring at
the picture  causes the retina to become fatigued and unable
to adjust quickly when your gaze is shifted.)

The skin on the back of your hand cannot differentiate between one touch and two touches.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Bend a paperclip into a U shape so the tips are about 6–7mm apart.
2  Ask your partner to close his/her eyes and stretch out one hand, palm up. Then lightly touch the two
tips onto your partner’s fingers near the fingertips. (Your partner will feel two distinct touches.)
3  Turn your partner’s hand over and explain that you will
now touch the skin with either one or two tips. (When you
use two tips your partner will only feel one.)
EXPLANATION
Some parts of your skin have relatively few pressure receptors. In these areas, the spaces in between the
receptors are insensitive to touch. The front of the hand, and especially the fingertips, have many more
touch receptors than the back of the hand.
TO INVESTIGATE
Which parts of your skin are least sensitive to touch? (Your face and fingertips contain many touch
receptors, but the upper arm, the small of the back and the back of the hand have far fewer.)
A normal person has more bacteria on their skin than there are people on Earth.
Your perspiration contains some urea (although most of it is in your urine).
LINKED ACTIVITIES

proportions of these in the class. (The pattern of ridges on the skin helps to increase friction when you
are holding on to things. The normal population is 65% loops, 30% whorls, and 5% arches. Every finger
of every person, including identical twins, has a unique print.)

Stick some clear adhesive tape over the print, then peel the

from a full set of inked prints of all the staff. (The pattern of
a fingerp

You can watch a snail make waves.
HOW TO DO IT 
1  Put a snail in a dish with a little water to encourage it to
come out of its shell.
2  Put the snail onto a sheet of damp clear plastic (e.g., from
an overhead projector). As the snail is moving across the
plastic sheet, look at it from the underside. (A series of
waves will be flowing forwards along its foot.) Safety
warning: wash your hands after handling specimens.
EXPLANATION
Each time one of the ripples reaches a muscle it contracts and lifts a small part of the foot, which is then
carried forward and set down. In this way the snail is propelled forwards.
TO INVESTIGATE
Can a snail move along the edge of a safety blade without cutting itself?
You should be glad you’re not a snail. A snail’s anus is located just above and just behind its head.
Snails have both male and female sex organs. Before copulation one snail fires a hard calcium ‘love
dart’ into the body of the other snail, then both snails donate sperm.
Our garden snail, Helix aspersa, is considered a delicacy in parts of Europe and the Middle East.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Look a snail in the eyes. Observe what happens to a snail’s
eyes (which are located on the long tentacles) as it emerges
from its shell. (The tentacles extend without the eyes, then
the eyes travel up the tentacles to the tips.)
2  Solve the following problem. Does each snail have a
unique shell pattern? How would you classify the types of
patterns on their shells?
3  Examine other molluscs. Obtain specimens of mussel and
oyster (in their shells), squid and octopus from a fish shop,
and a slug from the garden. What features would you use
to classify them into different groups of molluscs? (Snails
and slugs have a distinct head; mussels and oysters have a
shell in two parts; and cephalopods have several tentacles.)

You can make sounds with a straw.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Flatten the end of a soft plastic straw and cut the two
corners off so there are two points at the end. 
2  Close your lips firmly over the end of the straw, so the
points are just inside your mouth, and blow into the straw.
Safety warning: sit down and hold the straw firmly to
prevent it being pushed too far into your mouth by accident.
(With a bit of practice you will make a loud, buzzing
sound.)
EXPLANATION
When you blow, the points vibrate like the reeds in a clarinet. This makes the column of air inside the
straw vibrate. The pitch of the sound depends on the length of the column of air.
TO INVESTIGATE
What would happen if you used a pair of scissors to cut the straw in half while you were still blowing?
To play the didgeridoo properly, you need to breathe in and blow out at the same time. 
The column of air in a French horn can be over 5 m long.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a bird whistle. Make a cut in a straw and bend it as
shown in the diagram below. As you puff intermittently
through the horizontal section, move the vertical section up
and down in the water. (The sound will become more high-
pitched when there is a shorter column of air vibrating inside
the vertical section.)
2  Amplify a Bunsen burner. TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY
Laboratory coat and heatproof gloves should be worn. Light a
Bunsen burner and carefully lower a galvanised pipe over it. 
(The sound of the Bunsen burner will resonate inside the pipe.)

Only a small part of this ruler is on the table, but it still doesn’t fall to the ground.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Use a length of string to loosely tie a ruler to a hammer. 
2  Position the end of the ruler on a table top, so the head of the hammer is suspended under the table.
(The ruler will not fall.)
EXPLANATION
An object is balanced if its centre of gravity is on, or just
below, the point where it is supported. In this case, the head
of the hammer is very heavy, so the centre of gravity of the
system is somewhere below the edge of the table.
Scientists still don’t know what causes gravity.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa is in genuine danger of
collapsing, but it has not yet been decided how to save it.
It leans over 5 m off centre.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Suspend a potato. Insert a matchstick and two forks (with
heavy handles) into a potato so that it is suspended from
the corner of a bench, as shown in the diagram. (The heavy
handles of the forks cause the centre of gravity to be located
near or under the bench top.)
2  Find the centre of gravity of Australia. Cut out a cardboard
shape of Australia, hang it from a pin, and mark the
direction of a plumb bob hanging from the same pin. Move
the pin to another part of the shape and mark the direction
again. The centre of gravity is where the two lines meet.
Which town is closest to it? (Australia doesn’t really have a
centre of gravity, but this technique can be used to find the
centre of gravity of an irregularly shaped object.)

A tuning fork will make water splash up.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Strike a tuning fork firmly.
2  While it is still ringing strongly, dip the tips of the prongs
into some water in a plastic cup. Don’t let the prongs touch
the sides of the cup. (The water will splash up.)
EXPLANATION
The sound of the tuning fork is made by vibrations of the
prongs. The water splashes when energy from the vibrations is
transferred to the water. 
TO INVESTIGATE
What do the vibrations of a tuning fork do to a ping-pong ball?
How would you use an overhead projector to observe the
vibrations of a tuning fork?
Giraffes do have a voice, but it is used so rarely that for many years scientists assumed them to be
completely incapable of vocalising.
A stockwhip makes a sonic boom. When a stockwhip cracks, the tip of the whip is travelling faster
than the speed of sound, and there is a crack as it breaks the sound barrier.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a cellophane whistle. Cut a piece of cellophane
about 3cm square, making sure that one edge is straight.
Pull the straight edge taut between your hands, hold it to
your mouth and blow firmly onto the edge. (The blowing
air makes the edge of the cellophane vibrate with a high
frequency, making a high-pitched whistle.)
2  Make a bullroarer. TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY — Make a hole at one end of 1m rule. Cut
1metre of strong string and tie one end to the hole (securely!). Hold the other end of the string and
whirl it around your head. Safety warning: this activity should be done outside the classroom in a
location where students can observe without risking injury if the string breaks. (The rule will vibrate as it
moves through the air, producing a loud whirring sound.)

This plant can move fast enough to catch insects.
HOW TO DO IT
1  Buy a potted Venus flytrap (Dionaea) from a nursery.
2  Find a pale-coloured trigger hair on the inside surface of a
trap and gently touch it with a pin. (The trap will close.) 
EXPLANATION
As venus flytraps are green plants, they produce their food by photosynthesis. However, they are often
found growing in poor soils, so they use their insect prey as a supplementary source of minerals,
especially iron and phosphorus compounds.
TO INVESTIGATE
If a trap closes without having caught any prey, will it open up faster than one that has caught prey (such
as a dead ant)?
Plants make up about 90% of the mass of all living things
on earth.
Most of the oxygen in the air is produced by microscopic
algae in the oceans, rather than by land plants. 
The earth’s forests are being cut down at a rate of about
40 hectares per minute. A lot of the wood is used to 
make toilet paper.
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make leaf rubbings to record differences between dicotyledons and monocotyledons. Place a sheet of
paper over the leaf and lightly colour the top of it with the side of a soft crayon. (The shape of the leaf,
and its veins, will become clearly visible.)
2  Locate the stomata. TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY
Lower a freshly picked gum leaf into a beaker of water that
has just boiled. (The lower surface of the leaf will become
covered with tiny bubbles, but the upper surface will have
few or none. The air inside the leaf has expanded from the
heat. Some of it appears outside the stomata, most of which
are on the lower surface.)

Wire mesh can hold water.
HOW TO DO IT
Hold a dry wire kitchen strainer over a sink. Carefully put 2 or
3 drops of water into it. (The water will stay in the strainer.)
EXPLANATION
Water is held in the mesh by adhesive forces between the wire
and water and cohesive forces within the water. A layer of
water forms in each hole in the mesh and the surface tension
stops the rest of the water from passing through. 
TO INVESTIGATE
What would happen if you put some detergent in the water? What would happen if you used oil or
methylated spirits instead of water? (Safety warning: be careful of methylated spirits’ fumes.)
If you hold a piece of canvas up to the light, you can see that it has lots of tiny holes in it, yet 
it still manages to keep the rain out. When it rains, the first drops of water seal the holes, so the rest
of the water runs off. But the Golden Rule of Canvas Tents is: don’t touch the inside of the tent when
it is raining. If you do, adhesive forces between the water and your finger will drag the water into 
the tent. 
LINKED ACTIVITIES
1  Make a raft from fly wire. Cut out a triangular shape from
a sheet of fly wire. Gently lower it onto the surface of the
water in a beaker. (The raft will float because the water
seals all the holes. You can observe this by lifting it out of the
water.) Add a few drops of detergent to the water. (The raft
will sink because the cohesive forces have been weakened by
the detergent.)
2  Make a fly wire bottle top. Cover the mouth of a bottle
with a layer of fly wire and fasten it with a rubber band. Fill
the bottle with water. (The water will go straight through
the fly wire.) Quickly tip the bottle upside down.(The water
will not run out because the water has sealed the holes in
the fly wire and air pressure exerts a force that counters the
weight of the water.)

A handful of forest litter can conceal a surprising number of these creatures.
HOW TO DO IT
TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY
1  Cut away one side of a milk carton to make a rectangular
viewing tray. Put a handful of mixed leaf litter (bits of dry
leaves and bark) in one half of the carton and leave the
other half empty. 
2  Collect 50 healthy woodlice (slaters) from leaf litter or
under paving stones and logs in the garden. Safety
warning: wear sturdy gloves because poisonous spiders also
inhabit these areas.
3  Place all the woodlice on the litter and give them 2 minutes
to hide.
4  Ask the students to observe the box and estimate the
numbers of woodlice inside. (They will usually

EXPLANATION

63) ELECTRICITY FROM A KIWI FRUIT

You can make electricity with fruit.

HOW TO DOIT

THEME: ELECTRIC CELLS

1 Use wires to connect a copper plate to one terminal of a microammeter and a zinc plate to the other.

2 Cut twoslits, about 2cm apart, in a kiwi fruit.

3. Insert the two metal plates into the slits. (The microammeter will indicate a flow of current.)

copper,

EXPLANATION

The zinc attracts electrons from the citric acid in the kiwi fruit
so it becomes negatively charged. The copper donates
electrons to the solution and becomes positively charged. The
difference in charge causes electrons to flow through the wire
from the zinc to the copper.

TO INVESTIGATE

Do some fruits generate more current than others? To what
extent is the amount of current influenced by the depth of the
electrode in the fruit?

terminal; after a minute or so a blue colour will appear at
the wire connected to the positive terminal.)

2 Solve the following problem. Is it possible to recharge a flat
battery by leaving it in the sun for a while? Design an
experiment to test this question.

3 Solve the following problem. Battery manufacturers
sometimes claim that their products last longer than those
of other brands. Test their claims by inserting batteries into
electrical toys (or other devices with moving parts such as
battery shavers) and comparing the time taken to run down.
Calculate the brand that offers the best value for money.

Historica NOTE

One of the scientists who helped to
develop batteries was Robert Bunsen.
While doing research in chemistry, he
nearly died from arsenic poisoning
and lost the sight of one eye in a
laboratory explosion.

If a dark stain is found at a crime scene, it may be blood belonging to either the victim or criminal.
Or it could be something else, like furniture polish or another dark stain. Before sending a sample to
the lab for testing, the Crime Scene Examiner must first establish that the stain is blood. For this
reason, a presumptive blood test is done. This is a test that is quick and simple to carry out at the
crime scene, confirming that the stain might be blood and so deserves further investigation.
There are two common ways such a test is done. In many countries a KM (Kastle-Meyer) or LMG
(leucomalachite green) test is done. In Australia, forensic investigators use a ‘hemastix’. This is
simply a plastic strip with a small square of special indicator paper attached to one end. Details of
both procedures are described below.

phenolphthalein (Kastle-Meyer or KM) solution

hydrogen peroxide

a number of small pieces of filter paper

pipettes, if solutions are not in dropping bottles
Alternatively, use a number of hemastix.

some dark brown or maroon stains, including dried animal blood, on a white ceramic tile

stain in the centre. Add a drop of

| Searching the crime scene .. --.. - .. > ..

Name

When a crime has been committed, there are specially trained police officers who are called out to search a
crime scene for clues. These officers are called crime scene examiners (CSEs). They look for evidence (evidence
is what the clues are called) that untrained people might not notice. These officers wear gloves, and overalls
made of a fabric that does not shed its fibres. Often they also wear elastic caps and overshoes, similar to those
worn in hospital operating theatres, so that they don’t leave any small particles (trace evidence) from
themselves at the scene.

The CSE will usually photograph the scene
first, then use a strong torch to inspect the
scene in more detail. Tweezers are used to
pick up small items that may have been left
behind by the criminal. If a smudge of
fingerprints is found on a hard surface, it
will be dusted using a special powder.

Any shoe prints or impressions left by tyres
at the scene are photographed, then a plaster
cast is made of each impression. These
photographs and casts can then be compared
to prints made from the suspect's shoes

or tyres.

Sometimes hairs or tiny fibres from a
criminal's clothes are found. These are
collected and sealed in specially labelled
bags, and then sent to the forensic laboratory
for further testing.

The police hope that this evidence will lead them to the person or people who carried out the crime, and will
provide enough information to convict the guilty person(s) ‘beyond all reasonable doubt’.

Some of the most common examples of trace evidence left behind at a crime scene
include hairs from a criminal’s body and fibres shed from their clothes. This is why | [= EEE
hairs and fibres are searched for, very carefully. As they are so small, a criminal would nylon

not even notice that they had been left behind.

A forensic scientist who specialises in hair identification can discover from which type
of animal the hair came, and - if the hair is human - which part of the body the hair | -~7— ZY SET
came from. Microscopic examination can indicate whether the hair was pulled out, | ” wool

cut off or just fell out naturally. Chemical tests can sometimes reveal any drugs or
poisons the person took, any hairdressing treatment like dyes and bleaches or in some
cases, even the foods eaten by the person. If there are any cells on the hair roots, then
a DNA profile can be made from the cells and the person identified if their profile is

on police records.

Fibres are classified as either synthetic (man-made), such as nylon and polyester, or
natural. If natural, they might come from plants such as cotton or from animals such
as sheep (wool) or caterpillars (silk).

Synthetic fibres are usually produced from a syrup-like liquid that dries into a long
thin filament of uniform thickness and colour. These filaments can be spun together
into thread. In the laboratory, samples can be compared using chemical tests to see if
they are made of exactly the same substances. Strength comparisons can be made by
measuring the force needed to break the thread, or melting points can be compared.

Natural fibres are far less uniform in their appearance. Their quality depends on the
health of the animal or plant and even on the seasons in which it grew. To identify |, -———>,-~
the type of natural fibre, inspection under a microscope is usually done first. Dyed

samples can also be matched using ultra-violet (UV) light,

Recording shoe prints and tyre marks ..

It is amazing how often impressions are left at a crime scene. They might
be from the tyres of a ‘get-away’ vehicle, or from a criminal’s shoes. Even
the tools used to break into a building can leave impressions on a
windowsill. When pressed on by an object, soft garden soil, mud or timber
will remain in the shape it was forced into by that object - and so leave
an impression.

When an impression is found, it is photographed with a strong light
source coming from one side. This ensures that the ridges and depressions
show up clearly. The photo on the right was taken with light coming from
the left, and you can see the small shadow that is cast near the edges of
the impression. A ruler is included in the photo so that the exact size of
the shoe is clear, even if the photo is later enlarged.

As well as taking a photograph, crime scene examiners make a cast of the
impression, using a substance like plaster of Paris if the impression is
large. The plaster mixes quickly and easily to a smooth paste that is
poured into the impression. For smaller impressions such as tool marks,
silicone rubber is used instead of plaster. After a short
time, the investigators working on the crime will have
a three-dimensional copy of the object that made the
impression. If they then find a similar object, such as a
shoe belonging to a suspect, they can compare it to the
photograph or cast to see if they match.

Using chromatography to compare inks - .. -- .. acTIviTy 3

Name

The inks found in pens are made from a number of different chemicals.
These chemicals are combined to give the desired colour and consistency
needed to leave a clear line on a page of paper. Different manufacturers
use slightly different combinations of these chemicals to produce their
inks, so each brand of pen has its own unique formula.

The chemicals in different inks can be compared using the simple
technique of chromatography. A sample of the ink is placed about 1 cm
from the bottom of a piece of absorbent paper, which is then stood in a
beaker that contains a small amount of solvent, such as water or
methylated spirits. The solvent slowly soaks up the paper. As it meets the
ink, some of the chemicals in the ink will dissolve and be carried up with
the solvent. This leaves a trail of different colours spread up the paper.

Some of the chemicals consist of very small molecules, and these will be carried furthest up the paper,
especially if they are very soluble. Where the ink chemicals are made of larger molecules that are less soluble,
these will not be carried as fast or as far up the paper. Each ink usually leaves its own unique pattern of
colours, called a chromatogram. If two chromatograms have the same colours in the same order, it is highly
likely that both samples came from a pen of the same type and brand.

Today in the forensic laboratory, chromatography is not used as described above. Instead, scientists use
instruments that measure the exact chemicals found in a mixture. A small sample of the substance is placed
in a chamber where it is heated so that it evaporates as a gas. The types of particles in the gas are identified,
and the scientist can print out a graph that shows the type and amount of each particle in the sample.

An individual's handwriting is unique and the way it appears on paper depends on the interaction of the
brain, eye and hand, Its appearance is also affected by the writer’s physical and emotional state, the
position in which he or she is writing and the type of pen or pencil being used.

The following is a list of things that a handwriting expert would look at when comparing two samples
of handwriting:

* How high and low the letters are in relation to a horizontal line

* The average space between the words and some letters

* The pressure and flow of the writing

* The slope of the writing (It can be backhand \\, normal /// or upright ||)

* The style of the writing (for example, cursive, printing or block letters)

* The style of certain letters (a or a, f or f, g org, t or t)

Experts that analyse handwriting can tell if a person is right-handed (pulls the pen across the page) or
left-handed (pushes the pen across the page).
