Before the twentieth century, it was almost impossible for a criminal to be convicted of a crime unless he
or she was ‘caught in the act’ or identified by an eyewitness. However, in the early 1900s solving crimes
started to develop into a science, which involved police closely examining the place where a crime was
committed, They looked for clues or evidence that might lead them to discover who committed the crime.

For this to be successful, the crime scene must be as close as possible to the condition it was in when the
offender (the person who committed the crime) left. If the scene is interfered with, it is possible that clues
or evidence could be destroyed or accidentally carried away by innocent people. Extra evidence that has
nothing to do with the crime could also be left behind,

To avoid this, examining the site should be left to experts because they have been trained to look for the
smallest pieces of evidence without doing any damage. They look for hairs, fibres, fingerprints invisible to
the eye, small spots of blood and more obvious evidence, such as shoeprints or tyre impressions.

These experts wear special protective clothing that does not shed fibres. They stand on duckboards to avoid
touching the floor. They also wear hairnets, overshoes and gloves so that they don't leave anything of them-
selves behind, Small objects are picked up with tweezers and then placed into special bags. These bags are
sealed and labelled with the type of object, the date, where the item was found and by whom. This evidence
is then transported to the forensic laboratory where it is closely inspected or tested by experienced scientists.

A membrane is the essential protective covering of a cell. Membranes separate one cell from another. All living
organisms are made up of cells; so membranes are essential to all life. The cell membrane is made up of a
phospholipid bilayer in which protein molecules float. The membrane also contains cholesterol molecules,
which give the membranes some rigidity and water resistance. Any factors that distort or alter proteins and lipid
molecules affect the permeability of the membrane.
Beetroot cells contain a pigment called betacyanin in their vacuoles. A special membrane called the tonoplast
surrounds the vacuoles. When beetroot cells are subjected to variation in pH, detergent, alcohol and high
temperatures, the pigment will leak out because these factors alter the tonoplast and cell membrane structures.
Variations in pH and high temperatures affect the protein molecules in the cell membrane. Detergent and alcohol
solutions disrupt the phospholipid bilayer.

O S M O S I S
Diffusion is the passage of molecules from a region of high concentration through a semi-permeable membrane
to a region of low concentration. Osmosis is the passage of water from a region of high water concentration to
a region of low water concentration. Semi-permeable membranes are very thin layers of material which
allow smaller molecules such as water, potassium iodide and glucose to pass through them, but prevent larger
starch molecules from passing through. In a hypertonic solution, the solute concentration is higher than that
in cells. In a hypotonic solution, the solute concentration is below that in cells. In an isotonic solution, the
solute concentration is equal inside and outside the cell.
In this experiment, dialysis tubing is used to demonstrate the action of a differently permeable membrane. When
plant cells are placed in hypertonic solution, they lose water and become flaccid. When plant cells are placed
in hypotonic solution, they gain water and become turgid. In an isotonic solution, cells are unchanged
because the amount of water leaving the cell is equal to the amount of water entering the cell.

Part A – Effect of catalase on hydrogen peroxide

To investigate the effect of catalase from different animal and plant cells on hydrogen peroxide.

Write a hypothesis to explain how catalase reacts with hydrogen peroxide.

A F F E C T I N G
C A T A L A S E
A C T I V I T Y
Enzymes are globular proteins. They act as catalysts that speed up chemical reactions without being
destroyed or altered during the process. Enzymes are extremely efficient and may be reused. Enzymes are specific
and react with a particular substrate. A substrate is a molecule with which the enzyme reacts and produces
products. The active site is the only part of the enzyme that reacts with the substrate. However, its unique
protein structure under certain circumstances can easily be denatured.
Some of the factors that affect enzyme reactions are enzyme concentration, pH, temperature, substrate and
product concentration, activators and inhibitors. Enzymes react best at optimum temperature and optimum pH. If
the environment of the enzyme is too acidic or too basic, the enzyme may irreversibly denature until it no longer
has the necessary shape for proper functioning. The enzyme tested in this experiment is catalase, an
intracellular enzyme. It is produced by cells to prevent the accumulation of toxic hydrogen peroxide. Hydrogen
peroxide is decomposed by catalase to water and oxygen. This reaction occurs spontaneously without catalase,
but the enzyme speeds the reaction considerably.

Equipment
SAFETY ISSUES
 When carrying a microscope, always use one hand to hold the arm and your other hand to support
the base.
 Never use cloth or paper products to clean the lenses. They will scratch the coating and decrease the
resolving power of the lens. Only use lens paper.

being scratched by the slide.
I N T R O D U C T I O N
T O
L I G H T
M I C R O S C O P E
Microscopes have enhanced our knowledge in basic biology, biomedical research, medical diagnostics and
material science. The most widely used microscopes are optical microscopes. These microscopes use visible
light to create a magnified image of an object that is too small to be seen with the unaided eye.
The compound light microscope uses two lenses, an objective lens and an ocular lens. The two lenses are
mounted at opposite ends of a closed tube to provide greater magnification.
Magnification is the extent to which the image of a specimen is enlarged when being viewed under the
microscope. The total magnification of a light microscope can be more than 2000 times.
The resolving power of a microscope is the ability to see two objects that are close together as separate
objects; that is, the ability to observe details. Light microscope usually has a limited resolution of between
200–250 nm. This means that any two points closer than this will appear to be one point.
The area of the slide that you see when you look through a microscope is called the field of view. If you know
the width of the field of view, you can estimate the size of the things you see in the field of view. When
switching from low power to high power, the area in the field of view gets smaller and darker. As the
magnification increases the field of view decreases.

O B S E R V I N G
C E L L S
According to cell theory, cells are the smallest functional units of life. All living organisms are composed of cells
and cell products. Two basic types of cells are prokaryotic cells and eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotic cells have a
more primitive (pro) nucleus (karyo) without a membrane. Bacteria and blue-green algae are prokaryotic cells.
Eukaryotic cells have true (eu) nuclei (karyo) enclosed by a nuclear membrane. Plant and animal cells are
eukaryotic cells.
Plant cells have cell walls and large vacuoles. Only photosynthetic cells have chloroplasts. Potato and
banana cells store starch in leucoplasts. Coloured plant cells have chromoplasts. The movement of cytoplasm
around the vacuole of a plant cell is known as cytoplasmic streaming. This enables cell products to be carried
to different parts of the cell.
Animal cells do not have any chloroplasts or cell walls. Some animal cells do not have vacuoles; if vacuoles are
present they are smaller in size. Human red blood cells do not have nuclei. This means that they have more
surface area for carrying oxygen and they bend easily when passing through fine capillaries. The red blood cells
of a frog have nuclei when they mature and divide. The white blood cells of frogs are similar to human in both
form and function.
Staining cells enables us to view cell organelles more clearly. However, the cells are killed during this process
because stains are toxic to cells.

To use a model to investigate:
• The effect of size and shape on SA:V ratio.

EFFECT OF SURFACE AREA TO VOLUME RATIO ON CELL SIZE
Most cells are microscopic in size because as a cell gets larger, it needs more food and produces more waste.
Therefore, more materials must be able to move into and out of the cell through the cell membrane. To keep
up with these demands, a growing cell needs a larger surface area through which to exchange materials. As
the cell’s volume increases, its outer surface grows too. However, the volume of a cell increases at a faster rate
than the area of its outer surface. As the size of the cell increases the surface area to volume ratio
decreases. Materials must be able to reach all parts of a cell quickly. When volume is too large relative to surface
area, diffusion cannot occur at sufficiently high rates.
The shapes of cells can also affect the amount of surface area of a cell. Cells that are spherical in shape have a
large surface area to volume ratio and are more efficient in obtaining nutrients, gases and getting rid of wastes.
However, cells come in a great variety of shapes. Rod-shaped cells have more surface area compared to their
volume than spherical cells.
In this experiment, the cell models are made of agar which has an acid-sensitive dye, phenolphthalein,
incorporated into it. The dye changes from pink to clear in the presence of acid. The uptake of acid and hence
colourless areas of the cell models represents the uptake of nutrients by the cell.

To ensure the continuation of the species, plants and animals use two methods of reproduction – sexual and
asexual. Sexual reproduction involves the fusing of two gametes, one from each partner, to form a new being.
Asexual reproduction does not require a second partner. One or more offspring are produced from only one
parent by the process of mitosis.
Vegetative reproduction is the propagation of plants using vegetative tissues such as stems, leaves and
roots. This results in a plant that is genetically identical to the original plant. In some species, stems arch over
and take root at their tips, forming new plants. For example, the horizontal above ground stems (runners or
stolons) of the strawberry produce new daughter plants at alternate nodes. Underground stems such as
rhizomes, bulbs, corms and tubers are used for asexual reproduction as well as for food storage.
Leaves of bryophyllum produce tiny plantlets along the leaf margin. Some plants like dandelion use their roots
for asexual reproduction. Plants can be propagated asexually by taking stem cuttings and by grafting. Animals
also reproduce asexually by various means.
Budding: The offspring develop as a growth on the body of the parent. In some species, such as jellyfish and
many echinoderms, the buds break away and take up an independent existence. In corals, the buds remain
attached to the parent and the process results in colonies of animals. Budding is also common among parasitic
animals such as tapeworms.

C L A S S I F I C A T I O N
O F
A N I M A L S
Taxonomy is the branch of biology dealing with the identification and naming of organisms. Classification is
the arrangement of objects, ideas, or information into groups, the members of which have one or more
characteristics in common. Scientific classification groups all plants and animals on the basis of certain
characteristics they have in common. During the 1700s, Swedish botanist Carolus Linnaeus classified all the
organisms that were known at that time into two large groups: the kingdoms Plantae and Animalia. Linnaeus
also developed the concept of binomial nomenclature whereby scientists speaking and writing different
languages could communicate clearly. In 1969, Robert Whittaker proposed five kingdoms: Plantae, Animalia,
Fungi, Protista, and Monera.
There are seven traditional major levels in a classification scheme. The kingdom is the group that contains the
largest number of different organisms. Kingdom is divided into further levels of phylum, class, order, family,
genus and species. Species can be defined as a group of organisms that is capable of interbreeding and
producing fertile offspring under natural conditions.
The animal kingdom is divided into vertebrates and invertebrates depending on whether they have vertebral
columns or not. Vertebrates are divided into five main groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Invertebrates are divided into the following phyla: porifera, cnidaria, platyhelminthes, nematoda, annelida,
mollusca, arthropoda and echinoderms.

The original purpose of biological classification was to organise the vast number of known plants into categories
that could be named, remembered and discussed. Kingdoms are divided into a hierarchical system of
categories called taxa (singular: taxon). The taxa are: phylum (usually called division in botany), class, order,
family, genus, and species. Intermediate divisions, such as suborder and superfamily, are sometimes added
to make necessary distinctions. The lower a taxon is in the hierarchy, the more closely related its members. The
species is the fundamental unit of classification. It consists of populations of genetically similar interbreeding or
potentially interbreeding individuals. The genus (plural: genera) is a grouping of similar, closely related species.
Green plants include all organisms commonly known as green algae and land plants. These include liverworts,
mosses, ferns and other non-seed plants, and seed plants. Plants are divided into two main groups according to
whether or not they have vascular tissue. This is the main tissue that transports water (xylem) and food
(phloem) for the plant. It is usually found when plants become more specialised, such as conifers and flowering
plants. The major phyla of the Plant kingdom are bryophyta (mosses and liverworts), filicophyta or
pteropsida (ferns), coniferophyta (conifers), angiosperms (flowering plants) and gymnosperms (non-
flowering plants). Angiosperms are again divided into monocotyledons (have one seed leaf) and
dicotyledons (have two seed leaves). Fungi are plants which have no chlorophyll. They are placed in a
separate kingdom, the

CONSTRUCTION OF A DICHOTOMOUS KEY FOR ARTHROPODS
Dichotomous keys are constructed to identify known and unknown animals, plants and other organisms. This is
based on a series of choices between alternative characteristics. For example, noting whether animals have
vertebrae or do not in order to divide animals into two main groups. Similarly, plants can be divided into two
groups by noting whether they have vascular systems or do not.
A dichotomous key for arthropods can be constructed by looking at characteristics such as the presence or
absence of an external shell or exoskeleton, the number of legs and body segments. Arthropods are joint-footed
animals that possess a hard, armour-like outer skeleton. Arthropods comprise about 95% of all known animal
species, and all but 5% of arthropods are insects. Non-insect arthropods include the class Crustacea (water-
dwelling crabs, shrimp, crayfish and lobsters), and land-dwelling isopods or sowbugs; the class Diplopoda
(many-legged, worm-like millipedes); the class Chilopoda (centipedes); the class Arachnida (mites, ticks, spiders,
scorpions, and harvestmen), the class Xiphosura (horseshoe crabs); and the extinct class Trilobita (trilobites).

Food is digested in the digestive system with the help of digestive enzymes. These enzymes are secreted by
the cells lining the inner surfaces of various glands of the digestive system. Amylase from the salivary glands
and the pancreas digest starch to maltose in the mouth and small intestine. The optimum pH for pancreatic
amylase is 6.7 to 7.0. Proteases are enzymes that break down proteins to polypeptides. Pepsin is secreted in
the stomach and its optimum pH is 2. Trypsin is secreted by the pancreas and its optimum pH is 7–8. Fat is
digested by pancreatic lipase in the intestine into fatty acids and glycerol. Bile from the liver emulsifies fats,
so that lipase has an increased surface to work on. This action takes place in the small intestine. The optimum
temperature for all these enzymes is 37°C.

Dissection is a technique used to study the internal organs of a dead animal. It shows the internal structure of
the animal, how the tissues look and feel, and how they are interrelated. All mammals possess similar organs
and systems whether they are small or large in size. To understand the structure and functions of our own
systems, it is helpful to dissect smaller mammals such as rats.
As rats are herbivorous, they have four long, sharp incisors for gnawing and twelve molars for chewing. They
have no canines or premolars. The toothless space between the incisors and molars is called the diastema. Their
digestive system is similar to that of humans except that they have a proportionally longer small intestine, a
large caecum to digest cellulose and no gall bladder. There are no differences between human and rat excretory
systems. The female rats have a V-shaped uterus that can hold many foetuses, whereas the human uterus is
smaller and usually holds only one foetus at a time.

right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle. The right side of the heart is separated from the left side by a
thick muscular wall called a septum. The left atrium-ventricle valve is known as the bicuspid or mitral valve.
The right atrium-ventricle valve is known as the tricuspid valve. This valve allows blood to flow only in one
direction: from the atria to the ventricles. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body via the
superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava. The blood then flows to the right ventricle and from there it
is carried to the lungs by the pulmonary arteries.
The lungs are pale pink in colour and feel firm and spongy. The left lung is divided into two lobes: the upper
lobe and the lower lobe. The right lung is divided into three lobes: the upper lobe, middle lobe and lower lobe.
When humans breathe in, air enters through the nostrils and goes to the pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi

the blood in the capillaries and air in the alveoli. Oxygen rich blood is carried back to the left atrium by the
pulmonary veins. The blood then enters the left ventricle and is pumped out of the heart via the aorta.
The liver is a reddish brown organ which is divided into two lobes: the right and the left. The right lobe is about

Scientists use two methods to survey the plants in a community, the transect method and the quadrat method.
A quadrat consists of a square, rectangular or circular frame which is used to identify and calculate the
abundance of plant species within a given area. Rectangular quadrats with a width-to-length ratio of 1:2, 1:4 or
1:8 are commonly used.
Transects are lines or belts that are set out in an area to study the type and abundance of a species. A line
transect is made by laying out a tape measure or a rope marked at regular intervals along the area to be
studied. The name and position of plant species are recorded and profile diagrams are drawn to scale. Belt
transect is made by laying out two parallel lines to define the area to be studied.

HOMEOSTATIC CONTROL OF TEMPERATURE AFTER EXERCISE
Thermoregulation is the ability of an organism to keep its body temperature within certain boundaries, even
when the temperature of the surroundings is very different. This process is known as homeostasis. Homeostasis
is the ability of an organism to maintain a stable internal environment irrespective of changes in either the
external or internal environment. In animals, homeostasis is controlled by hormonal and nervous systems.
Negative feedback mechanisms tend to produce stability. They act to restore the original state of the
organism. They are stimulus-response mechanisms, where the response produced affects the stimulus. Humans
are homeotherms and maintain body temperature in the range 36.1°C–37.8°C. During exercise, the body
produces more heat, carbon dioxide and wastes and the demand for oxygen and glucose increases. As the body
temperature increases, the temperature receptors in the skin and the hypothalamus detect the changes in
temperature. The thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus sends electrical impulses to the effectors via
motor nerves. The blood vessels near the skin dilate and heat is lost. The sweat glands produce more sweat and
heat is lost when the sweat evaporates from the skin. The response is a decrease in temperature until normal
body temperature is regained. This response affects the original stimulus by the negative feedback system. The
heart rate and breathing rate also increase to provide more oxygen and glucose to the exercising muscles. The
percentage increase in the heart rate is influenced by a person’s age, physical fitness, gender, size and emotions.

The tapeworms belong to the phylum platyhelminthes and the class cestoda. Taenia solium is the pig
tapeworm. It uses humans as its primary host and pigs as its secondary host. Taenia saginata is the beef tapeworm.
It uses humans as the primary host and cattle as the secondary host.
An adult tapeworm has a knoblike head, or scolex, equipped with hooks and suckers for attaching to the intestinal
wall of the host; a neck region; and a series of flat, rectangular body segments, or proglottids, generated by the
neck. The chain of proglottids may reach a length of 7 metres in T. solium and 12 metres in T. saginata. The adults
have an average of 1000–2000 proglottids. Terminal proglottids break off and are excreted in the faeces of the host,
but new ones are constantly formed at the anterior end near the neck. They have a rudimentary nervous system and
excretory system and have no digestive tract. They absorb the host’s digested food through their cuticle, or outer
covering. Each proglottid contains a complete set of male and female reproductive organs (hermaphrodite) that
produce the sex cells. Fertilisation is internal and about 50 000 eggs are produced per proglottid. The eggs are stored
until the proglottid detaches from the tapeworm, migrates to the anus and is excreted

Background

In the mid-1800s, Gregor Mendel experimented with how traits are passed from parents to their offspring. He
discovered that hereditary determinants (genes) are discrete entities that do mot mix in offspring. He also
found that genes have different forms (e.g. dominant or recessive) and that they pass from parent to offspring
according to the laws of probability. He chose common garden pea plants to be the focus of his research
because they are easily grown in large numbers, their reproduction can be manipulated and they have obvious
traits such as flower colour, seed colour, seed shape, pod colour, pod shape, flower position and plant height,
Mendel selectively cross-pollinated purebred plants that had a particular trait, and observed the outcomes over
many generations. A cross between plants with one pair of contrasting traits is called a monohybrid cross.
When pure-breeding plants homozygous for dominant and recessive traits were crossed, the offspring of the
first generation (F1) always had yellow peas, However, the following generation (F2) consistently had a 3:1 ratio
of yellow peas to green peas. Mendel found similar results for other contrasting pairs of characteristics, When a
hybrid plant was test crossed, it produced 2 phenotypes in the ratio of 1:1.

A dihybrid cross involves studying inheritance patterns for organisms that differ in two traits. When two hybrid

NATURAL SELECTION IN PEPPERED MOTHS

Timing: 2 x 45 minute lessons

Background
The peppered moth, Biston betularia, occurs in two forms: f. typica (fight form) and f, carbonaria (dark form).
150 years ago, the species consisted almost entirely of ‘typical’ forms. They had predominantly light grey scales
interspersed with black scales. This gave the moth the name ‘peppered’. The Industrial Revolution in Britain
began in the 1840s. During this time, a large amount of airborne pollution was produced, in the forms of soot
and toxic gases. This pollution killed the lichen on the bark of trees growing in industrialised areas.

By the 1950s, at least 90% of peppered moths living in polluted areas were dark in colour. The melanism shown
by peppered moths is known as industrial melanism. This is because it is caused by the soot from industry,
Researchers noted that the increase of the proportion of dark moths paralleled the increase in industrial
pollution, They hypothesised that the dark moth was better camouflaged than the light moth when they settled
‘on soot-darkened tree trunks. These observations suggested that the light moths were removed from the
population by birds because they were more conspicuous than the dark moths. Additional support for this
hypothesis came from non-industrial regions where the light moths greatly outnumbered the dark moths, In
these areas, the selection was reversed and the light moths had the advantage in hiding from birds on the
lichen-covered tree trunks.

selection. The Hardy-Weinberg Law provides 2 mathematical formula for calculating the frequencies of

M E I O S I S
Meiosis occurs in sex cells to form gametes (sperms and ova). Meiosis is divided into two parts: meiosis 1 and
meiosis 2. During meiosis 1 and meiosis 2, the cell goes through four stages for each nuclear division: prophase,
metaphase, anaphase and telophase. Meiosis 1 is known as the reduction division, because the two
daughter cells that are formed at the end of this process receive half the number of chromosomes (haploid) of
the parent cell (diploid). During prophase 1, homologous chromosomes (consisting of maternal and paternal
chromosomes) pair up (synapse). Crossing over can occur between two non-sister chromatids and genetic
material is exchanged. Crossing over produces genetic variation, the raw material for evolution. Meiosis 2 is
similar to mitosis. At the end of the meiosis 2, four haploid daughter cells are formed which become the
gametes. Meiosis provides genetic variation. This gives organisms the ability to adapt to changing environments
and also assists the process of evolution.

Part A – Examining a prepared slide of an onion root tip
In plants, mitosis takes place in the apical meristems. These are normally found at the tips of the stems or roots.
The root consists of a root cap, a zone of cell division, a zone of cell elongation, a zone of cell differentiation and a
zone of maturation. At the tip of the root there is a thimble-shaped cap called the root cap. This protects the root
from the soil grains. Meristem is the region just behind and partially covered by the root cap. It is in this region that
the new cells divide by mitosis. In the zone of elongation, the cells become longer. In the zone of cell
differentiation, cells differentiate in size and shape. In the region of maturation, the cells become mature and
carry on with various functions.
Aim
To observe and identify different stages of mitosis in a slide of an onion root tip.

‘Chromosomes are thread-like structures found in the nucleus of a cell. They are made up of
deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins. Genes are sections of chromosomes that code for proteins and
the inherited instructions that control structure and function. The deoxyribose sugar molecule of the DNA
backbone has 5 carbon atoms and 3 oxygen atoms. The carbon atoms are numbered 1’, 2', 3°, 4° and 5’, The
hydroxy! groups on the 5'- and 3°-carbons link to the phosphate groups to form the DNA backbone.

DNA is made up of sub-units called nucleotides. A nucleotide consists of one nitrogen base, one phosphate
group and one deoxyribose sugar molecule, There are four different nitrogen bases: adenine, cytosine,
guanine and thymine. Adenine and guanine are purines, Cytocine and tyrosine are pyramidines. The number
of purine bases always equals the number of pyrimidine bases. Adenine always pairs with thymine and cytosine
always pairs with guanine. The nucleotides make up two chains that are linked and twisted around each other in
the form of a double helix.

DNA replication begins with a partial unwinding of the double helix at an area known as the replication fork.
This unwinding is caused by the enzyme DNA helicase. As the two DNA strands separate, the bases are
exposed. Then the enzyme DNA polymerase moves into position at the point where synthesis will begin.
Nucleotides are added, one by one, in an exactly complementary manner: adenine to thymine and guanine to
gytosine.

Background

Protein synthesis involves two processes: transcription and translation, During transcription, a small section
of the DNA double helix unwinds and the bases of the two strands are exposed. The DNA strand that is
transcribed is called the template strand or sense strand, The DNA strand that is not transcribed is called the
fon-sense strand or antisense strand.

During transcription, RNA polymerase enzyme binds to the DNA molecule at a region known as the promotor
site. This site is in front of the gene where transcription will begin. A gene consists of coding regions called
exons and non-coding regions called introns. RNA nucleotides (ribonucleotides) line up in the proper order
by hydrogen-bonding to their complementary bases on DNA. DNA that includes all the exons and introns of the
gene is first transcribed into @ complementary RNA copy called nuclear RNA. Then introns are removed from
the nRNA by a process called RNA splicing, This edited sequence Is called messenger RNA or mRNA, mRNA
Moves from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and attaches to a ribosome. Three-dimensional, inverted cloverleaf-
shaped molecules called tRNAs are present in the cytoplasm. At the top end of tRNA, a specific amino acid can
be attached with enzymes called aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. At the lower end, the tRNAs carry
anticodons which are complementary to mRNA codons.

Translation occurs at ribosomes in the cytoplasm. As protein synthesis begins, one small sub-unit and one

of the mRNA acts as a ‘start’ signal for the translation and codes for the introduction of a methionine

Topic 4 
1 
The need to classify chemicals into 
different groups:
a is unnecessary if chemicals are simply 
listed in alphabetical order.
b comes about because there are so many 
(millions!) of chemicals.
c reflects the history of their discovery.
d is based on the relative importance of 
the chemicals.
2 
As chemicals are classified into different 
groups, the important principle is that the 
chemicals within a particular group:
a have similar physical properties, such 
as mass and colour.
b are usually in the same state, i.e. all 
liquids or all solids.
c have chemical formulae which start 
with the same element, e.g. HCl and 
H2O.
d have many chemical properties in 
common.
3 
One broad classification of chemicals is to 
put them into two groups called ‘organic’ 
and ‘inorganic’. The original classification 
into these groups generally meant that:
a organic chemicals were those found in 
living things, while inorganic chemicals 
were nothing to do with living things 
and were found within the rocks and 
the atmosphere of the Earth.
b only food products were included in 
the group called ‘organic’.
c only minerals such as iron ore and 
aluminium ore were classified as 
inorganic chemicals.
d the points in B and C were the critical 
ones.
4 
A simple classification of chemicals is to 
put them into two groups called ‘elements’ 
and ‘compounds’. When this system is 
used: 
a the ‘compounds’ group would have 
many more chemicals in it than the 
‘elements’ group.
b the ‘elements’ group would have 
many more chemicals in it than the 
‘compounds’ group.
c the group called ‘organic’ chemicals 
would be left out.
d most of the ‘inorganic’ chemicals would 
not be included.
5 
The group of chemicals which we call 
‘compounds’ all consist of:
a two elements combined together.
b either two or three elements combined.
c a number of different elements 
combined.

Topic 1 
Elements and 
atomic structure
1 
Modern atomic theory:
a is based on the idea that all substances 
are composed of small particles.
b recognises that even atoms are 
composed of smaller particles.
c explains why a particular amount of 
one chemical will react with a definite, 
set amount of a second chemical.
d embraces all of the above ideas.
2 
In the 1600s, before atomic theory was 
recognised, it was thought that:
a two reacting chemicals could do so 
regardless of the amounts of each.
b the term ‘atoms’ only applied to some 
chemicals.
c any elements which reacted with one 
another would do so in the ratio of 1:1.
d only metals like silver and gold were 
made up of atoms.
3 
The development of the atomic theory is 
usually accredited to the scientist:
a Lavoisier.  
b   Dalton.
c Davy. 
 
d   Einstein.
4 
The original proposal(s) in the early 
atomic theory included the idea(s) that 
‘atoms’:
a were present in all substances.
b could easily be divided into smaller 
particles.
c represented the smallest ‘indivisible’ 
particles present in all matter.
d had the properties of both A and C 
above.
5 
One difference between early atomic 
theory and the more modern version is 
that the early version considered that 
atoms were:
a able to be ‘split’, whereas the modern 
version says that they are indivisible.
b not involved in chemical reactions, 
while it is now known that they are.
c tiny individual ‘solid particles’, while 
the modern version considers all atoms 
to be mainly space.
d tiny individual ‘solid particles’, while 
the modern version considers atoms to 
be larger than originally thought.
6 
The reason the atomic theory is called a 
‘theory’ is that:
a it has more evidence to support it than 
a hypothesis would have.
b the evidence to support it is stronger 
than if it were called a scientific law.
c atoms have actually been seen with the 
aid of modern light m

Topic 12 
1 
People should be concerned about ‘heavy’ 
metals because, in larger quantities, they 
are not readily eliminated from the body 
and can cause health problems. Three such 
metals are:
a sodium, potassium and lithium.
b sodium, potassium and lead.
c mercury, lead and zinc.
d lithium, zinc and calcium.
2 
In the movie Erin Brokovich, it was shown 
that a particular chromium compound 
was responsible for horrendous health 
problems as people unknowingly absorbed 
the compound in their daily lives. And yet 
chromium is an essential element for our 
bodies. The fact that chromium can cause 
major health problems probably means 
that:
a only very small amounts are needed for 
the healthy functioning of our bodies.
b it is some other metal associated with 
chromium that causes the health 
problems.
c it is only when the chromium is in 
a concentrated form and absorbed 
continually by our bodies that it 
becomes a health problem.
d both A and C are true.
3 
A problem with heavy metals, even if they 
are present in very tiny amounts in living 
things, is that:
a they accumulate via the food chain.
b plants tend to accumulate them more 
than animals.
c only carnivorous animals can eliminate 
them.
d they give very bad tastes to food.
4 
Industrial plants called ‘smelters’ fuse or 
melt metal ores in order to extract the 
metals. For example, to produce zinc, 
the ore ‘sphalerite’ (ZnS) is roasted in air 
to produce zinc oxide (ZnO). The oxide 
is then heated strongly with carbon to 
produce the metal. The equations for the 
reactions are:
Step 1.  2ZnS(s) + 3O2(g) → 2ZnO(s) + 2SO2(g)
Step 2.  2ZnO(s) + C(s) → 2Zn(s) + CO2(g)
 
The effect of these processes would be to:
a produce gases which are acidic oxides.
b use a lot of oxygen from the air for 
heating.
c use a lot of energy to produce the metal 
zinc.
d do all of the above. 
5

smelters i

which can be found in their ‘native’ or 
elemental states in nature. Three such 
elements include:

1 
The use of indicators in chemistry:
a is restricted to acid/base reactions.
b mostly involves a chemical which 
can change colour in the presence of 
another type of chemical and so reveal 
its presence.
c involves only organic chemicals which 
can change colour.
d involves only inorganic chemicals.
2 
A common indicator used in the 
laboratory is phenolphthalein. It is red/
violet in alkali but becomes clear in an 
acid solution. If a student added some 
clear phenolphthalein to a clear liquid in a 
beaker and no colour change occurred, it 
would mean that:
a the liquid in the beaker must be acidic.
b phenolphthalein is not a suitable 
indicator in this situation.
c the liquid in the beaker is water.
d the liquid in the beaker is definitely not 
a strong alkali.
3 
Indicators such as methyl orange, litmus 
and phenolphthalein are commonly used 
with acid/base reactions. This is because 
they:
a are readily available and easily made 
into solutions.
b are safe to use in school situations 
providing that standard precautions are 
implemented.
c have the properties of both A and B 
above.
d all undergo similar colour changes in 
acid/base reactions.

© Grahame Dobinson and Blake Education 2008
Topic 10 
1 
The main reason for processing chemicals 
is to:
a ensure that they are not poisonous.
b make an end product that has suitable, 
desired properties.
c lower the cost of making the chemicals.
d make them totally inactive and safe to 
handle.
2 
An alloy is a type of mixture, usually of 
two elemental metals. For example, brass 
is an alloy of mainly copper and zinc. 
‘Stainless steel’ is an alloy of steel and 
chromium. The property of stainless steel 
that is the reason for its manufacture is 
that it:
a does not oxidise in the air and so does 
not rust as iron does.
b is extremely malleable and can be 
shaped more easily than most other 
metals.
c is much lighter (i.e. less dense) than 
iron.
d has less iron in it than pure iron and so 
is cheaper to produce.
3 
The smell of the interior of a new car is 
mainly due to chemicals called plasticisers. 
These chemicals are present in vinyl 
and ‘synthetic leather’ upholstery and 
escape over time. The ‘plastic’ of a biro 
or a hard cutting board would not have 
these plasticisers to such a large degree. 
The reason for using these plasticisers is 
probably to:
a give the property of flexibility to the 
vinyl or plastic.
b ensure that the vinyl or plastic is safe 
for humans.
c make the plastic or vinyl hard and 
strong.
d make the plastic or vinyl more dense.
4 
When margarine is originally made, it 
is not the colour that we see in the final 
product. A yellow additive is put into it 
before it is presented for sale. The most 
likely reason for this is to:
a make the margarine have a soft texture.
b make the margarine have a more 
agreeable taste.
c preserve the margarine as yellow 
additives are the best preservatives.
d give margarine an appearance similar 
to butter.
5 
The chemical sulfur dioxide (SO2) or other 
chemicals which release sulfur dioxide 
are commonly added to foodstuffs and 
recorded as ‘additive 220’.

1 
Some chemical reactions occur very 
rapidly while others may take extremely 
long periods of time to complete. An 
example of (a) a very fast reaction and  
(b) a very slow reaction would be:
a (a) the rusting of iron, (b) the 
dissolving of iron in a dilute acid.
b (a) the reaction between hydrogen and 
oxygen, (b) the rusting of iron.
c (a) the reaction between hydrogen and 
oxygen, (b) the reaction of sodium 
metal with water.
d (a) the dissolving of zinc in dilute acid, 
(b) the combustion of a hydrocarbon 
fuel such as petrol.
2 
If any chemical reaction is to proceed at 
even a moderate rate, then it would be 
necessary for the reactants to be:
a extremely reactive chemicals.
b heated vigorously.
c mixed fairly thoroughly to allow them 
to be in contact.
d in the gaseous state since this is the 
only state where the amount of mixing 
will allow a reaction.
3 
If copper (or brass, which contains copper) 
is exposed to the air, it slowly ‘tarnishes’ 
or changes colour with time, even though 
copper is a fairly inactive metal. This 
probably means that:
a the copper reacts very slowly with some 
component of the air.
b the copper must have some impurities 
in it for it to behave this way.
c acids in the air are responsible, since 
only they can cause metals to tarnish.
d nitrogen in the air reacts with the 
copper.  
4 
Iron and sulfur are two solid elements 
which do react when heated with one 
another to form the compound iron 
sulfide. However, if a single solid piece 
of iron with a volume of about 1cm3 is 
placed in sulfur powder and heated, there 
is only a very small amount of iron sulfide 
produced. The best way of increasing the 
yield of iron sulfide would be to:
a flatten the piece of iron to make it 
thinner.
b dissolve the iron in a concentrated acid 
prior to mixing with the sulfur.
c dissolve the sulfur in a suitable solvent

When an element such as sodium reacts 
with an element such as chlorine, the two 
elements:
a react in any proportions with no  
‘left-overs’.
b sometimes form a compound and 
sometimes form a mixture.

proportions by mass.
d only react if there is three times the 
amount of chlorine as there is sodium.
2 
When sodium reacts with chlorine and 
the formula of the resulting compound is 
written as NaCl it means that:
a 1.0 g of sodium reacted with 1.0 g of 
chlorine.
b 1 atom of sodium reacted with 1 atom 
of chlorine.
c 1 molecule of sodium reacted with  
1 molecule of chlorine.
d the formula NaCl simply shows the 
elements present and has nothing to do 
with amounts in the reaction.
3 
The formula NaCl suggests that the bond 
formed between sodium and chlorine is 
probably:
a an ionic bond since sodium is a metal 
and chlorine is a non-metal.
b covalent because chlorine forms mainly 
covalent bonds.
c a very weak bond since it involves a 
metal and a non-metal.
d an ionic bond, but could be a covalent 
one, depending on how the NaCl was 
formed.
4 
In any chemical reaction between two 
elements, each element shows a ‘combining 
power’ or valency which:
a is usually 1 or 2.
b is usually 1, 2 or 3 but never greater 
than 3.
c varies depending on the masses of the 
elements involved.
d is fairly characteristic for each element.
5 
Whatever number is given to an element’s 
valency (e.g. 1, 2, 3) it is a measure of the 
number of:
a hydrogen atoms which one atom of the 
element could combine with.
b oxygen atoms which one atom of the 
element could combine with.
c grams of a second element which could 
combine with 1.0 gram of the first.
d molecules of hydrogen which 1 
molecule of the first element could 
combine with.
6

If a chemical reaction is described as one 
which is ‘spontaneous’, it means that when 
the chemicals are mixed, they:

the case of zinc metal and dilute

In coal mines, explosions have occurred

trapped in the coal has been released and 
becomes mixed with air. This means that:

components in the air.
c the reaction is not a spontaneous one

without an explosion occurring.
d methane gas is extremely reactive with 
most common reagents.

The chemical reactions which are called 
decomposition reactions, such as those 
involved in extracting a metal from an ore, 
are:
a rarely spontaneous as most of them 
need the addition of energy to make 
them proceed.
b mostly spontaneous because they 
usually form elements.
c mostly spontaneous except for a few 
which need heat to start them off.
d spontaneous when they involve a metal 
compound.
4 
Examples of spontaneous reactions in 
chemistry include:
a active metals reacting with common 
dilute acids.
b non-metals such as sulfur reacting with 
metals such as iron.
c any reaction between two non-metallic 
gases.
d all of the above.

connected to a battery as shown, electricity

Topic 2 
1 
When scientists first found ways of 
comparing the masses of atoms, they used 
the mass of the hydrogen atom as a basic 
unit of ‘one’. This was because: 
a using ‘grams’ or even ‘milligrams’ as 
units was not practical.
b the hydrogen atom was the one with 
the smallest mass.
c it meant that atoms of every other 
element would have masses greater 
than one.
d all of the above statements were 
applicable and true.
2 
If we say that ‘a helium atom has an atomic 
mass of 4’, then we are saying that:
a each helium atom has a mass of 4.0 g.
b an atom of helium has 4 times the mass 
of a hydrogen atom.
c each atom of helium has a mass of  
4.0 milligrams.
d four atoms of helium have the same 
mass as one atom of hydrogen.
3 
The original Periodic Table was formed as 
a result of scientists arranging the elements 
in order of increasing atomic masses and 
noticing that:
a there was a regular (or periodic) repeat 
of elements which had very similar 
properties.
b elements with names starting with the 
same letter had similar properties.
c only metallic elements had similar 
properties.
d only non-metallic elements had similar 
properties.
4 
The modern Periodic Table arranges 
elements in order of increasing:
a atomic mass, just as the original one 
did.
b densities of the elements.
c atomic number, which is the number of 
protons in the nucleus of each atom.
d atomic number, which is the combined 
number of protons and neutrons in the 
nucleus of each atom.
5 
In the modern Periodic Table, the metallic 
elements tend to be found:
a towards the left side of the table.
b towards the right side of the table.
c only at the top of the table.
d scattered equally throughout the table.
6 
The modern organisation of elements in 
the Periodic Table puts elements which 
have similar chemical properties:
a in horizontal rows across the table.
b in vertical columns down the table.

Topic 5 
1 
Perhaps the simplest type of chemical reaction is a combination reaction. It usually involves 
elements, or even compounds, bonding together to make a new compound. Three chemical 
reactions are listed below.
 
 (i)  magnesium(s) + oxygen(g) → magnesium oxide(s)
 
(ii)  sodium(s) + chlorine(g) → sodium chloride(s)
 
(iii)  calcium carbonate(s) + heat energy → calcium oxide(s) + carbon dioxide(g)
 
Of the three reactions, the ones which are combination reactions are:
a (i), (ii) and (iii). 
b   (i) and (ii). 
c   (i) and (iii). 
d   (ii) and (iii).
2 
If a combination reaction does not occur between two chemicals, it could mean that:
a both of the chemicals are inactive.
b only one of the chemicals is inactive.
c one chemical could have a protective coating, e.g. an oxide, which prevents it from reacting.
d any of the above options might be true.
3 
When the element helium is mixed with the element argon and the mixture is heated strongly, 
there is no evidence of a combination reaction occurring. This is due to the fact that:
a the mixture has not been heated strongly enough to cause a reaction.
b the proportions of helium and argon are incorrect and so no reaction occurs.
c both elements are always extremely unreactive.
d while helium is quite an active element, argon is not.
4 
Four combination reactions between metals and non-metals which occur quite readily are:
 
(i)  potassium(s) + fluorine(g) → potassium fluoride(s)
 
(ii)  sodium(s) + chlorine(g) → sodium chloride(s)
 
(iii)  magnesium(s) + oxygen(g) → magnesium oxide(s)
 
(iv)  sodium(s) + iodine(s) → sodium iodide(s)
 
This is because in every case:
a there is an active metal and an active non-metal.
b the metal is an active one, even though the non-metal is inactive.
c the non-metal is an active one, even though the metal is inactive.
d the metals are in the solid state, otherwise there would be no reaction.

 your TASk – You are an investigator for the Australine Insurance Company. Two days ago  
(Tuesday 17th) an accident occurred involving a bicycle and a motor vehicle insured by Australine. 
Fortunately, neither the motorist nor the cyclist was seriously injured (the cyclist sustaining only a 
sprained ankle and minor leg and head injuries). However, the motor vehicle was badly damaged when, after 
clipping the bicycle, it careered into a street sign. The motorist has put in a claim for the cost of repairing 
his vehicle. The cyclist has also put in a claim for the replacement of her bicycle and her medical costs, 
arguing that the motorist was totally to blame for the accident.
This activity tests your ability to read with understanding, to think logically, and to express yourself clearly and 
concisely. Merely knowing the correct answer to the main question is not enough. You also need to explain how you 
arrived at your conclusion, and on what evidence you based your decision.
follow these steps
1 
 Read your task and study the maps, then write on your report a list of some likely causes of the accident.
2 
Read the accident reports submitted by the driver of the motor vehicle and the cyclist.
3 
Distinguish facts from opinions.
4 
Look for points of agreement among the various reports.
5 
 Determine the single most probable cause of the accident, and list the supporting evidence on which your 
decision is based.

 Your TaSk – You have been employed by the Calthorpe Private Detective Agency to investigate  
a theft from the Luxor Motor Company. The plans and specifications for the latest model of its top  
selling sports sedan, the Luxor Lambretta have been stolen, despite the most stringent security 
precautions. The design of the vehicle is revolutionary, taking a range of automatic operational functions 
to a completely new level, and setting the performance standards for at least the next decade. Should 
the plans fall into the hands of an unscrupulous rival company, the marketing advantage of a billion dollars 
of research and development (R&D) may be lost. Your job is to find out who stole the plans, how the crime 
was carried out, and whether the plans are still in the car plant.
This activity tests your ability to read with understanding, to think logically, and to express yourself clearly and 
concisely. Merely knowing the correct answer to the main question is not enough. You also need to explain how you 
arrived at your conclusion, and on what evidence you based your decision.
follow these steps
1 
 Read your task, the notes on the structure and operation of the Luxor Motor Company, and Donna O’Brien’s 
interview statement. Think about how you would go about committing such a crime, given the tight security 
measures involved.
2 
 Examine the employee list. Look for any connections that might point to the identity of the individuals 
involved.
3 
 See if you can figure out the methods by which the safe’s combination number and the DVD passwords were 
derived.
4 
 State who you think committed the crime, what their motives were, and how the crime was carried out.

 Your TaSk – Since his Mum has been unwell, the job of organising his older brother Dheran’s  
twenty-first birthday party has fallen to Jarrah. It is a big responsibility, and one that Jarrah really  
wants to get right. His family is not wealthy, and while Dheran said that he didn’t want anything special 
or too expensive, Jarrah knows that his mum wants her sons’ twenty-first birthdays to be occasions to 
remember. She has been putting aside a small amount of money each week over the years to make this 
possible. Dheran’s share only added up to five hundred dollars, but Jarrah feels that, with careful planning, 
he can put on a really good party for this amount. The trouble is – the weather.  
 
Hiring an indoor venue would put a big dent in the birthdy fund. Having the party during the afternoon at 
the outdoor function area at a local park would mean that Jarrah could spend more money on food and 
entertainment. He’d heard that weather in October was often unpredictable, and he knew that he’d have to 
decide about the venue well before the event. What should he do? 
This activity tests your ability to read with understanding, to think logically, and to express yourself clearly and 
concisely. Merely knowing the correct answer to the main question is not enough. You also need to explain how you 
arrived at your conclusion, and on what evidence you based your decision.
follow these steps
1 
Read your task.
2 
Read Jarrah’s diary entry.
3 
Read all the weather prediction information.
4 
 From this information, decide whether the party should be held outdoors or indoors, and explain your 
decision.

How does this statement support the warm-blooded theory?  
4. The range of structures on dinosaurs, such as the sails on the back of the stegosaur, 
have been identified as controlling body temperature. 
 
How does this statement support the warm-blooded theory?

sound & lIght Ideas
Aristotle’s idea was based on thinking, not experiments. Was he a scientist?
The Ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle (AD 384–322) conducted thought 
experiments to learn more about the world. One thing he thought was that sound 
and light travelled through air just like waves in the sea. He then concluded that 
light and sound was not able to travel without a material to carry the waves. 
1. What may have led Aristotle to these ideas?
2. In what ways are light and sound like waves in the sea?
3. In what ways was Aristotle right? What evidence do you have to support your ideas?
In the 1640s Evangelista Toricelli (1608–1647) succeeded in making a vacuum. It was 
then shown that Aristotle was wrong about light. A candle could be seen through a jar 
with a vacuum, therefore light could travel through a vacuum. It was not like water in the 
waves of the sea – it did not need a material to carry it.
4. What do you understand by the term ‘vacuum’?
5. What other evidence supports the idea that light does not need material to travel?
Robert Boyle (1635–1703) showed that sound could not travel 
through a vacuum. He placed a loudly ticking watch in a bell jar 
and then pumped out all the air. As the air was taken out, the 
sound of the watch ticking became fainter and fainter until it could 
not be heard at all. As he let the air back in, the sound of the 
ticking returned.
6. Explain why the ticking sound became fainter as the air was 
pumped out.
7. What did Boyle’s experiment show about how sound travels?
8. In space movies, spaceships are often shown flying past with a loud whooshing 
sound. What is wrong with that?

The students are trying to reason about the ‘cause and effect’ relationships 
between the parachutes’ features and performance. What do you think ‘cause 
and effect’ means? How do science experiments help link cause and effect?
Van and Alicia’s class is conducting rate-of-fall tests on parachutes they have 
made. They were hoping to use their tests to help them to improve their designs. 
It is easy to see when the weight pulling down is too great for the drag of the 
parachute. It is harder to reason about the relationship between the features and 
performance of a parachute that does work.
Van and Alicia think that close observation of 
parachutes as they fall will help them make design

factors.
1. Rate of fall – How fast does the parachute fall?

design?
2. Flight path – Does the parachute fall straight 
down, at an angle, or swing while descending? 
How does the flight path tell you about what to 
change in a parachute design?
3. Inflated canopy – Does the canopy remain fully inflated, or does it sometimes 
partially or fully collapse? 
How does the canopy inflation tell you about what to change in a parachute 
design?
4. Stability – Does the canopy remain balanced during descent, or does it list to one 
side, flip over or oscillate while descending? 
How might stability help in assessing parachute design?

Ecology is the study of the interactions of organisms with other organisms and with their physical environment.
Food chains and webs are often used to show these interactions. Plants are known as producers because
they use sunlight and inorganic materials to produce organic compounds. This occurs through the process of
photosynthesis, where light energy is converted into chemical energy. Animals that feed upon plants are called
primary consumers, while animals that eat other animals are known as secondary or tertiary consumers.
Scavengers feed on dead organisms. Decomposers and detrivores break down non-living organic matter
into materials that are then available to enter the food chain as nutrients.
A food chain shows how each living organism gets its food. A food web consists of many food chains which
are interrelated and divided into separate feeding groups or trophic levels. The trophic level of an organism is
its position in the energy flow pyramid of an ecosystem. A food pyramid helps us to visualise the fact that in
an ecological system there need to be many producing organisms at the bottom level of the pyramid in order to
sustain fewer organisms at the top level. Energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next trophic level in
a food chain and food web. When one organism consumes another, about 5–10% of the chemical energy is
transferred to the predator. 90% of energy is lost as heat energy to the environment. More pesticides and
insecticides accumulate in organisms at higher trophic levels. This phenomenon is known as biological
magnification.

= Timing: 2 x 45 minute lessons

The Galapagos Islands consist of 13 major islands. They are located in the Pacific Ocean, 1000 km from the coast
of Ecuador which is in South America. Charles Darwin's visit to the Galapagos Islands in 1835 was the Starting
point for his theory of natural selection. This theory describes a process by which organisms that have
favourable variations survive and reproduce at a higher rate than other organisms.

An inherited variation that increases an organism's chance of survival in a particular environment is called an
adaptation. The finches and the giant tortoises living on the Galapagos Islands are two examples of adaptive
radiation. This means that a single lineage has diversified into a variety of species that have different adaptive
features. Adaptive radiation is an example of divergent evolution,

Approximately 10 000 years ago, small finches (grass quits) travelled 1000 km across the Pacific Ocean from
South America to the Galapagos Islands. These islands were relatively free of competitors. The grass quits
underwent radiation, producing 13 species that occupy a variety of niches,

10 million years ago, the ancestors of the giant tortoises arrived in the Galapagos Islands by clinging to a piece
of wood that drifted from a river mouth on the Pacific coast of the South American mainland all the way to San
Cristobal Island. The tortoises then spread throughout the islands, When Darwin arrived, there were
approximately 300 000 giant tortoises on 11 of the islands, The tortoises on individual islands developed into
their own sub-species. This was due to the effect of the founder principle, genetic drift and natural
selection, These islands were isolated and the animals were subjected to different environmental conditions,
which resulted in their gradual evolution into different species.

COMPARISON OF PRIMATE FEATURES

nag Timing: 2 x 45 minute lessons

Primates evolved about 30 million years ago in Africa. One branch of primates evolved into the old world
monkeys and the new world monkeys. The other branch evolved into hominids, The hominids includes humans,
extinct species of human-like creatures and the great apes: chimpanzees (genus Pan), gorillas and orangutans
(genus Pongo). It has been estimated that humans diverged from gorillas about 8 million years ago, and from
chimpanzees about 5 million years ago.

Biologists betieve that chimpanzees are our closest evolutionary relatives because we have 99.4% of DNA in
common with them. The earliest genus of hominids is the Australopithecus, meaning ‘southern ape’. About 2
million years ago, as many as 6 hominid species evolved in response to climate changes associated with the
beginning of the Ice Age. Two major groups developed: the Australopithecines and the line that led to the genus
Homo. The Australopithecines were generally smaller brained and non-users of tools. They died out 1 million
years to 2-2.5 million years ago.

The line that led to the genus Homo was larger brained and were makers and users of tools. Homo habilis
evolved with a larger brain and different shaped skull and teeth, About 1.8 million years ago, Homo erectus
evolved and appears to have migrated from Africa into Europe and Asia. H. erectus had a larger brain, flatter
face and prominent brow ridges. H. erectus is similar to modern humans in size, but there are differences in the
shape of the skull, a receding chin, brow ridges and differences in teeth. Between 100 000 and 500 000 years
ago, H. erectus disappeared and was replaced by a new species, Homo sapiens.

PATTERNS OF EVOLUTION

Timing: 2 x 45 minute lessons

Background
Evolution can be defined as the change in the frequency of one or more alleles in 2 population's gene pool
from one generation to the next, due to natural selection, There are three main types of evolution: divergent,
convergent, and parallel.

In convergent evolution, unrelated species become increasingly similar in appearance because of a shared
environment. Convergent evolution results in analogous structures that carry out a similar function but are not
similar in basic structure, This is because they are not inherited from @ common ancestor. For example, sharks,
porpoises, and penguins are not related through a common ancestor, but they all have peripheral fins and bodies
that are similar in shape. These traits are a direct result of adapting to aquatic life. Similarly, wings developed
independently in insects, reptiles, birds and bats.

In divergent evolution, two or more species develop from a common ancestor. This happens through adaptation
to different environments, Divergent evolution results in homologous structures. These are shared by related
species because they have been inherited from a common ancestor. For example, the forearms of various
vertebrates are homologous because they have similar bone structures but different functions,

Parallel evolution is the development of the same characteristic in unrelated organisms through adaptation to
similar environmental conditions. For example, the marsupial mammals of Australia are similar to the placental
mammals from other parts of the world. However, marsupials in Australia evolved in isolation after Australia
separated from the other continents.

ANALYSIS OF HUMAN PEDIGREES

Back 7 - Timing: 2 45 minute lessons
The pattern of inheritance for many traits is worked out using pedigree analysis. A pedigree is a diagram of
a family that lists the members of the family and their relationships. The primary patterns of inheritance are
autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, sex-linked recessive and sex-finked dominant.

In autosomal recessive inheritance, the recessive gene is located on one of the autosomes. Unaffected
parents (heterozygotes) can produce affected offspring. The affected individual must be homozygous recessive.
This trait can be inherited by both males and females, and it can skip generations. Examples of autosomal
recessive inheritance are cystic fibrosis, thalassemia, Tay-Sachs disease and sickle cell anaemia, In autosomal
dominant inheritance, the dominant gene is located on one of the autosomes. Affected individuals must carry
at lease one dominant gene, which can then be passed on to both males and females, The inheritance of this
wait does not skip generations. Examples of autosomal dominant inheritance are Huntington disorder and
Marfan syndrome.

In sex-linked recessive inheritance, the gene is located on the X chromosome. More males are affected by
this type of inheritance than females, because males inherit the X chromosome from their mothers and the Y
chromosome from their fathers, Females can only inherit the trait if the father has it and the mother is a carrier.
if females are affected or carriers, they pass the gene to their sons. Males cannot be carriers. The inheritance can
skip generations, Examples of sex-linked recessive inheritance ate colour-blindness, Duchene muscular dystrophy
and hemophilia,

TYPES OF INHERITANCE

a“ Timing: 2 « 45 minute lessons

In genetics, dominance relationships are the ways genes interact to express themselves as phenotypes in an
individual. There are three kinds of dominance relationships. Simple dominance is where one gene's allele is
completely dominant over the recessive allele, The individual is thus a carrier of the recessive gene but the
recessive gene is not expressed at all. Incomplete dominance is where both alleles of a heterozygote
influence the phenotype. A cross between organisms with two different phenotypes produces offspring with a
third phenotype that is a blending of the parental traits. For example, when red snapdragon plants are crossed
with white snapdragon plants, they produce pink flowers.

Codominance is the situation in which a heterozygote shows the phenotypic effects of both alleles equally. A
cross between organisms with two different phenotypes produces offspring with a third phenotype in which both
of the parental traits appear together. Among the alleles controlling human A8O blood groups, the alleles for A
group and B group are codominant and are expressed in the offspring with AB blood group. The allele for O
group is recessive to both A and B alleles.

There are two types of sex linked inheritance: Sex-linked recessive inheritance and sex linked dominant
inheritance. In sex-linked recessive inheritance, the recessive gene is located on the X chromosome. If the
mother is a carrier, her sons will be affected by the trait and the daughters could become carriers, Colour

Examples of people’s attempts to produce replacement materials for impaired 
or lost body parts are scattered throughout history.  
1 
What is meant by impaired? 
Early Egyptians, Greeks and Romans all left evidence (artefacts) that illustrates 
their use of artificial limbs, including wooden noses! Silver and gold wires, 
bones, clay, skins and wood have all been used to repair injuries. Mummified 
remains dating back to 1100 bc (Egypt) have been identified as having stitches 
(sutures) in the body tissues, while plaster casts date back to at least 2000 bc. Many South American tribes took 
advantage of the large, sharp pincers found on soldier ants to ‘stitch’ surface wounds. The ants were placed on the 
open skin and became defensive, pinching the lips of the wound closed in an attempt to attack. Once the pincers 
were securely in place, the ant was pulled away and its pincers remained in the skin. 
Society’s reawakened interest in ‘natural remedies’ has recognised what American Indians, Australian Aborigines 
and ancient Egyptians have long known about the value of using honey to disinfect wounds. Evidence suggests that 
these people also used animal skins and/or clay mixtures to form casts. All of these things are early examples of 
biomaterials.

Microchip is a very familiar word used in bionics. Originally designed for computers, these tiny devices are now 
also used in home appliances, video cameras and televisions, and many other items. Even the family pet can have a 
microchip implanted (at the back of the neck) to provide ownership details in case they are lost. Microchips are also 
used in the operation of biomedical devices.

the science fiction fans, laser beams! The word laser is an acronym (a word formed by the first letter of a number 
of words) for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Lasers can direct extremely fine beams of 
electromagnetic radiation of a specific frequency, with great precision and intensity. Laser technology is commonly 
used in minimally invasive surgery. A laser beam can concentrate a lot of energy onto a very small area.

Heart disease can develop in different ways. Characteristics inherited from parents

Smoking is linked to many diseases, including heart disease. A heavy smoker who

provided other factors (such as heredity) do not play a role.

Other smoking-related conditions that can indirectly affect the heart include lung cancer, high blood pressure 
and, because of high levels of carbon monoxide (CO) circulating through the blood, cancers developing in major 
organs. A former smoker still has a high chance of developing cancers (though the risks are dramatically reduced 
by quitting) so it is most sensible not to begin smoking in the first place. Many public places are now smoke-free 
because ‘second-hand’ smoke (smoke exhaled by smokers) is highly toxic if inhaled. Constant exposure to second-
hand smoke can lead to cancer developing in a non-smoker.

Classifying diseases 
1
Disease is described as disorder in the normal, healthy functioning of a living organism. It is a condition that reduces 
health and well-being in some way. Diseases can be categorised into several groups. Two main classifications are 
acquired and congenital. 
Acquired diseases are those that people are not born with, but contract through other ways. While many of these are 
self-inflicted, such as smoking-related lung cancer and liver disease resulting from alcoholism, diseases can also be 
acquired through work and environmental conditions.
1

2

3 
Animals are not the only organisms that contract ‘illnesses’. Name a disease that affects the health of plants. 
 
Congenital conditions are those that people are born with. These conditions may be diseases or syndromes. A 
syndrome is a group of symptoms that occurs together to produce a particular disorder (Greek sundromē, meaning 
‘to run together’). Many people think that a syndrome, such as Down Syndrome (‘Trisomy 21’, the result of extra 
genetic material from chromosome 21), is not a disease. One argument for this is that individuals with Down 
Syndrome often display cheerful dispositions. However, individuals who have Down Syndrome show varying 
degrees of mental retardation and roughly 40% have serious heart defects. (The damage is determined by how 
much extra chromosome 21 the person carries and which genes are involved.) Some people argue that it should be 
classified as a disease condition because of this impairment to health.

Cells can be divided into two categories: somatic and gametic. Somatic cells are cells that make up body tissues, 
organs and all other parts of an organism, apart from the sex cells. Somatic comes from the Greek soma meaning 
‘body’. Gametic cells are sex cells, such as sperm and ova. The word comes from the Greek gamos meaning 
‘marriage’.  
Cells that have two of each type of chromosome are said to be diploid. Somatic cells are diploid (Greek diploos 
meaning ‘twice’). Haploid cells have only one of each type of chromosome, half the number that are present in 
diploid cells. Gametes are haploid (Greek haploos meaning ‘single’).

Monohybrid crosses are crosses that involve only a single phenotype. But in reality, crosses involve more than one 
physical characteristic. Mono means ‘one’ and hybrid offspring ‘of one race’, so monohybrids are those offspring 
produced from one phenotype. Crosses that involve two characteristics are called dihybrids. Di means ‘two’ so 
dihybrids result from crossing two phenotypes.

Fred Hollows (1929–1993): A man with a vision
Professor Fred Hollows is known and admired by many people for the incredible number of lives he improved by 
reducing blindness. Fewer people are aware that this New Zealand-born ophthalmologist (eye specialist) was the 
Head of a Sydney hospital’s Eye Surgery Department and a pioneer in the treatment of trachoma.
Fred Hollows was appalled by the number of Australian Aborigines suffering unnecessary blindness as a result 
of poor health and unclean living conditions. He set to work enlisting aid to save their sight. By the 1970s, he had 
reduced blindness in many Aboriginal communities by up to 50%. The cause of this blindness was Chlamydia 
trachomatis, a micro-organism with both viral and bacterial characteristics. C. trachomatis causes the condition 
trachoma, the main cause of human blindness around the world. The condition is extremely contagious, as the 
micro-organism is found in the runny ‘weeping’ discharge it creates as the eye becomes increasingly inflamed. The 
discharge is easily transferred to fingers, tissues and other surfaces. It also travels easily via flies as they move from 
person to person. 
This is an ancient condition, dating as far back as the Egyptian Pharaohs. It causes scarring on the fine membrane 
coating the inner eyelid and eye surface (conjunctiva). It is extremely painful and the inflammation and scarring 
continues until finally, if left unchecked, blindness results. Trachoma continues to be a problem in poor countries 
where sanitation, access to clean water and good hygiene are inadequate.
